Moreover, if the hon. member thinks that Ontario was relatively better supplied than other provinces with nails and other building materials, then he has been misinformed; because the point where the critical shortage of nails and other building commodities was most acutely felt, relatively -and when I say relatively, I mean in relation to the need-was in Ontario.
You did not answer the question. How did you build 10,000 houses if you could not get nails?
Order.

They were built in Ontario; and more houses would have been built if more building materials had been available, and if the efforts of those who were engaged in producing building materials, in distributing them and using them in construction, had not been hamstrung and hampered by the government that the hon. member was elected to support.

This is my concluding plea. Mr. Speaker, in order that the readers ot Hansard may be able to appreciate more fully
National Housing Act
the consistency of my good friends of the Progressive Conservative party, I should like for a moment to refer back to a little argument that developed in the house just before one o'clock between the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
That argument arose over a vote in the house on a C.C.F. amendment to a bill amending the National Housing Act in May of 1948. At some length this morning the hon. member for Eglinton gave his explanation for the action taken by his party in the vote on that amendment. Incidentally he described the amendment as tricky, and a socialistic tidbit. What are the facts as recorded in Hansard?
They are these. During the course of the debate several members on the Progressive Conservative benches, along with a number of C.C.F. members, argued that the government should make provision in that bill for subsidized low-rental housing. I have read a number of those speeches, and so far as I can discover both Progressive Conservative and C.C.F. members in that debate spoke almost the same language on the subject, and discussed subsidized low-rental housing in almost the same terms.
After the Progressive Conservative amendment to the bill had been ruled out of order, the C.C.F. moved an amendment on May 5, 1948, as recorded at page 3644 of Hansard- no, I should say it was moved on May 19 and is recorded at page 4164 of Hansard.
We can see who wrote the speech for him.

The amendment stated:
That Bill No. 280 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to providing subsidized low-rental housing.
I should like to read into the record a statement made during that debate by a member of the Progressive Conservative party who, among others, spoke in favour of subsidized housing. This is the quotation from a speech delivered on May 5 by the then member for Vancouver-Burrard, Mr. Merritt, as recorded at page 3644 of Hansard:
I believe that the basic reason for the change in the government's attitude is that it has refused to enter the field of subsidized low-rental housing for those in the low-income group. The minister knows it is not possible to provide rental housing at rents which those in the low-income group can afford to pay, unless this type of housing is subsidized.
And a little later he said:
I say to him-
-and he was speaking to the minister-
-that this is the time to face up to the problem of subsidized low-rental housing.

National Housing Act
And a little later:
There is nothing necessarily socialistic about subsidizing housing for the low-income groups. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and no other minister need ever worry about that. Subsidized housing for those with low incomes was introduced in Great Britain in 1920 by a Conservative government, and it has been in operation, and in useful operation, in the United States of America since 1938 or thereabouts.
Those sentiments are expressed in language very similar to that used by C.C.F. members and others in the house over the years. Then came the vote on the amendment, and every Progressive Conservative member who remained in the house tor the vote, including the hon. member for Eglinton, voted against it-I presume on the ground set forth this morning by the hon. member.
I submit that was not a tricky amendment. It was not a socialistic tidbit. It was as straightforward as any amendment moved by a private member on that particular bill could possibly have been. It was surprising therefore to find Progressive Conservative members voting as they did. Readers of Hansard will have to judge for themselves and reach their own conclusions. I submit however that Progressive Conservatives are in favour of subsidized low-rental housing, provided the measure is brought in by their own party. They appear to be so befuddled by their capitalistic free-enterprise thinking that they cannot even recognize something for which they themselves have asked when it is introduced by a member of the C.C.F.
I should like to make one further comment, since the hon. member for Eglinton chose to introduce provincial politics into the debate, just in case other hon. members from other provinces may gather from his grandiloquent expression of achievements of the Conservative government of Ontario that we have no housing problem in Ontario. Let me assure the house that, notwithstanding the fact that since 1943 we have had a Conservative government in Ontario, the housing situation in that province is just as acute as it is anywhere else in Canada. I believe I can say that the sole effective step taken by that government from 1943 to the present time to relieve the housing situation there has been the provision of second mortgage money to the purchasers of homes where the security was not sufficient to warrant their friends, the mortgage bankers and trust companies, to risk their money.
I will admit that householders who otherwise would not have been able to purchase homes have been placed in a position where they could purchase them-but those purchases have been made by tying around their necks another millstone in the form of second mortgages, a condition which may well lead

in the near future to a repetition of what happened in the thirties, when tens of thousands of home owners lost their homes and their investments, and when those same mortgage bankers and trust companies reaped a bonanza in the form of repossessed housing.
We have before us today the 1949 edition of the Liberal government's housing plan. As you know, sir, there was also the 1945 edition. That is the edition which was publicized during the election campaign in the spring of 1945. Hon. members opposite will undoubtedly recognize this little pamphlet which was prepared under the auspices of the national Liberal federation, Ottawa, and printed in Winnipeg. It is called, "New Housing Plan of the Liberal Government". It was new in the spring of 1945. It calls for the building of a new social order in Canada. A fine new building plan for Canada is pictured. On the front page is depicted a man holding a model of a house that was to be built for $3,000, and was to be purchased at $13.82 a month, plus municipal taxes. There was a cheaper house as well, one at $2,000, which was to be available at $9.58 a month. On the inside we are told how it works and what it means. We find this choice bit:
This plan means more and better homes for hundreds of thousands of families. It means closing the present gap between our housing needs and the number of homes available.
On page 3 we are told that the low-cost home ownership is just part of the housing plan. It says:
Legislation-
I do not know where the legislation was. This pamphlet told the electors in 1945:
Legislation also provides for low-rental housing.
There were to be houses for rent. There was to be slum clearance. There was to be a large-scale housing development. There were to be houses for farm families, houses for returned men, and there was to be a department of the government set up for development and research, and all this for $9.58 a month, and yet some people talk about the C.C.F. making promises and talking about pie-in-the-sky. I suggest that no Canadian citizen has ever been able to eat pie under the roof of any of these houses that had been built by the Liberal government since 1945 at either $9.58 or $13.82 a month.
When we begin to come to grips with this housing problem, sir, the first fact that confronts us is the shortage of houses. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) says the Conservative government in Ontario has done, notwithstanding all the glowing promises of the Liberal party in 1945 and again in 1949 there is still a tragic shortage of houses. The 100,000 units

which it is expected will be built this year will barely take care of this year's new requirements.
A report on the housing problem by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities estimates that today throughout Canada there are 300,000 more household groups than there are individual residential units. They go on to say that there is another 300,000 units still being occupied which, by modern standards of what constitutes good housing, should long since have been demolished.
Our present rate of housing, high as it may be compared with past years, is just not catching up on that backlog of 300,000 houses needed if our people are to find any kind of house, apart from providing replacements for the 300,000 no longer fit for human habitation. That is the first fact confronting us. At the present time we need 300,000 houses to provide any kind of homes for our people and another 300,000 to replace dilapidated houses that are now occupied.
The second fact is that the policy we have been following has, in effect, resulted in overbuilding for certain economic groups and under-building for others, and these others are those whose need is most acute, and who are unable to afford the rent or purchase price at the prevailing high construction costs. For this class, notwithstanding all the lavish promises we have had from the Liberal party since 1945, we are as yet building no houses at all. That is the second fact to be considered.
The third fact to be considered is that with the demand for housing at the prevailing high cost already beginning to fall off it is not reasonable to expect private building to go on creating a surplus big enough to provide any housing for low-income families. There again the federation of mayors points out in their report that lending institutions will no longer keep on financing projects for which there is no ready market. With these facts in mind it becomes self-evident that any housing bill which will adequately meet the need must do one or both of two things. First, it must provide for the building of houses at a price where the monthly purchase price or the economic rent comes within the ability of middle- and low-income groups to purchase or rent.
Second, it must provide a rental subsidy of at least $20 a month and build a minimum of 12,000 houses a year on that monthly rental subsidy basis for the next ten years.
I chose the figure 12,000 because the Canadian construction association says that available labour and building material are sufficient at the present time for the building of 12,000 low-rental dwellings a year for ten years, presumably without interfering in
National Housing Act
any way with our present policy of building high priced houses, as many of them as can be sold, and without interfering with the present policy of permitting the building of theatres, hotels, gasoline stations, beverage rooms, cocktail bars, factories, stores and so forth, that the market can absorb.
Or, third, such a bill must provide for a combination of lower costs and rental subsidies.
Now, sir, let us examine the principles of the bill before us with these points in mind. The bill does contain five provisions that are helpful-helpful to the extent that half a loaf is better than no bread. The first of these provisions is for a second loan which will reduce the down payment. Second, the extension of the amortization period from 25 to 30 years; third, a vague sort of control over the price, since the second mortgage is to be made contingent upon the selling price being reasonable, whatever that may mean.
Then there is a provision for building houses for rent in conjunction with the provinces; and lastly, the extension of national housing assistance to the co-operatives on a more generous scale.
The first and second provisions of the bill are designed to make it easier for the purchaser to make his down payment, and it spreads his payment out over an additional five years because of the increased mortgage. It does nothing whatever to reduce the cost of housing. As I have pointed out already, I fear that the result of the measure may well be, as in the case of Ontario, a repetition in the near future of the situation that faced us in the thirties when home owners, carrying mortgages larger than they were able to pay, lost their homes when they were repossessed by mortgage companies and banks.
One of the major factors in the cost of houses today is the interest charge, and the bill does nothing whatever to reduce it. We hear a great deal about feather bedding by certain groups of people. We hear that bricklayers are feather bedding, that they should lay more bricks, and that the building trade workers are getting too much wages. We do not hear about the feather bedding being done by real estate speculators and mortgage bankers. The biggest feather bed in Canada today is that on which the mortgage bankers are sleeping, and the bill does nothing to reduce the size of that bed.
To illustrate how interest enters into the cost of a house, I want to take the example of a $10,000 dwelling. I take that figure because it represents about the lowest priced house that can be bought in Toronto or the Yorks at the present time. Today $10,000 is the market price of a bungalow with two

National Housing Act bedrooms downstairs, and two unfinished attic rooms. If we take a $10,000 house carrying two mortgages, as provided for in the bill, and I presume bearing interest on both mortgages at 4| per cent over a period of thirty years, such a house, with a first mortgage to the extent of 80 per cent of the cost, $8,000, and a second mortgage which is one-sixth of $8,000, or roughly about $1,300, or a total mortgage of $9,300, will cost $15,900 when paid for, $5,900 more than the original cost. I suggest that if the same house were built with money bearing interest at 2J per cent amortized over thirty years, it could be purchased for $36.73 per month exclusive of taxes instead of $46.96, and would eventually cost the purchaser $13,222 or a saving of $2,700. If the same money were amortized at 2J per cent over forty years, compounded half yearly as I suggest in all these calculations, a $10,000 house could then be purchased for $30.60 per month exclusive of taxes, and would still cost the purchaser over $1,000 less on his forty-year payments than it would cost on the thirty-year payment plan at 4J per cent.
I am talking now about the middle income group, that percentage of our population now in receipt of incomes from $2,000 to $3,000 a year, and I submit that the government in any measure which attempts to provide for that class should reduce the interest payments to 2J per cent and extend amortization to forty years. As evidence that I am not being unrealistic, I want to call the following facts to the attention of the house. A labour press release from Washington dated November 4 indicates that members of the United States senate housing subcommittee, who have just returned from a tour of European housing, report that in Scandinavia government loans for co-operative housing are made at 2J per cent, about the cost of the money to the government, and that payments are spread over one hundred years on houses of brick and stone construction, and over sixty years on houses of wood construction. That is the report of the United States senate housing subcommittee.
The United States co-operative housing bill now before their senate calls for government loans at 3 per cent and amortization over a period of fifty years. In the United States public housing on a large scale has been built in the past with government money loaned at less than 2 per cent. In New Zealand 30,000 rental homes have been built with money loaned by the New Zealand government at from 1 to 14 per cent. As has been pointed out here, even the Conservative government of Ontario has been advancing government money at 3 per cent. The federal


government advances money to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at 2 per cent, and money to limited dividend companies at 3J per cent. Yet it insists on charging co-operative builders and others 4J per cent. Surely there is no justification for a government charging 4J per cent if it wants to bring housing even within the reach of the middle income group.
A noted United States authority, Nathan Strauss, writing in his book "Seven Myths of Housing", has this to say:
A reduction in financial charges, that is, interest and amortization, by half would effect a greater reduction in annual costs than cutting in half both the cost of labour and materials.
A Canadian authority, Leonard Marsh, writing in Public Affairs of October, 1947, says:
If the interest rate should be cut by one-third, say from 3 to 2 per cent, operation costs would be reduced 12 to 15 per cent.
The government proposes to place some check on the selling prices of houses on which there is a second loan. May I point out that in the bill the government appears to be making no attempt whatever to check profiteering on building materials, real estate speculation, or excessive profits by contractors. There is a widespread belief in Canada that building costs are unwarrantably high. I most strongly recommend to the government that they give heed to the request of Mr. A. R. Mosher of the Canadian Congress of Labour for a royal commission to go into the whole question of building costs. I submit that such a commission should investigate whether or not contractors are making excessive profits, whether or not the cost of building materials is unduly high, whether labour costs are unduly high, whether real estate interests are profiteering, whether interest rates can be reduced, and also whether the decentralization of the industry is making for higher unit costs than are necessary.
If the government is serious in its desire to provide homes for those people in the middle income bracket, receiving from $2,000 to $3,000 income, who can afford only $30 or $40 a month in payments or rental for housing, then I have three suggestions to offer. First is the extension of the amortization period to forty years; second, the provision of government money to builders, co-operatives, municipalities, and home purchasers at two and a half per cent. I can see no good reason why, in its effort to protect private enterprise, this government should refuse to lend money to people building in a metropolitan area, and lend only to those in outlying districts where loans have been refused by insurance companies. That seems to me to imply that this government is much more

concerned with protecting private interests who lend money than in having houses built for the people who need them. In the third place I suggest an acceptance of Mr. Mosher's suggestion for an investigation into the whole question of building costs.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the question of providing homes for the one-third of our people who cannot afford to pay more than $20 per month. According to an investigation by Dr. Leonard Marsh, as reported in a Star editorial some little time ago, 33-4 per cent of our people today are receiving less than $2,000 per year, even though their income is twice what it was in the pre-war years. Under instructions given by the government to those who borrow under the National Housing Act, one should not be required to pay more than twenty per cent of his gross income for housing, including rental or mortgage payments, taxes and so on. On that basis some 33-4 per cent of our people cannot afford to pay more than from $15 to $30 per month, and there simply are no houses available at those prices. I have here pages of advertisements from the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star taken last week end. Here are the rents being charged in Toronto today: five-room bungalow, one year lease, $150 per month; brand new five-room bungalow, $150 monthly to reliable tenants; fine large brick house, sixteen rooms, $200 a month; house on a quiet street near shopping, eight rooms, $125; four unfurnished rooms, new home, $100; five-room upper suite, $115; four and a half room upper duplex, $150. And so on. Those are about the only houses available in Toronto for rent today.
In view of what I have said in reference to the price of houses and the need for them I would ask the minister to indicate clearly to this house whether or not this bill provides for subsidized housing in the sense that a rental reduction fund will be established and a subsidy will be paid on rent for people in the lower income group. Does the bill provide for a subsidy on rent, or does it provide only for a subsidy on the cost of construction? In view of what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said about subsidized housing, in view of the vagueness of this bill, I think the minister owes it to this country to state in a forthright manner whether or not this legislation envisages a subsidized housing plan under which the difference between the economic rent and the rent people can afford to pay will be met by a monthly subsidy from a rent reduction fund. I think that is the most important question before us today. If the government does not visualize the construction of houses on that basis, I submit that by its recent action in connection with rentals the government is
National Housing Act
merely adding more confusion and more hardship to a housing situation that is driving hundreds of thousands of people to the point of despair. If the government were half as interested in building houses for people as they were in building an iron curtain around the McGregor report concerning flour, we would have houses available today for these people.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to submit that in view of the fact that rentals are invariably tied up with the whole question of housing, and in view of the fact that the federal government may soon pass out of the picture as far as rent control is concerned, consideration should be given by the government to rescinding the order concerning rentals which was made public a few days ago. At this point, with your permission, I desire to move the following amendment:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate and prior consideration to rescinding the order announced on November 3 providing for increases in domestic rents.
Mr. C. E. Johnston {Bow River): I wish to say a very few words on this occasion. The last time this matter was before the house I spoke at some length, but there are many points which I desire to discuss in detail when the bill is before the committee. I should like to take this opportunity of saying to the minister that I think the bill he proposes is an improvement on anything we have had up to date. There are a great many ways in which I believe the bill could be improved, but at least the government has taken one small step in that direction. There is necessity for a decided improvement in housing conditions in Canada.
It seems to me that now there is a greater need for housing than ever. If the effort were put forth that this problem deserves, I believe great strides could be taken in solving it. Whether or not the bill which is before the house will solve the problem remains to be seen. I notice that when the minister was speaking he gave figures to show that the housing condition was improving. In that connection, I should like to read an article published in the Ottawa Citizen which quotes the dominion bureau of statistics on the housing problem. The article is dated October 13 and reads as follows:
This was reported by the bureau of statistics yesterday in its monthly housing bulletin. It showed, however, that fewer new houses were started this year than last.
That is not in accord with the minister's statement. The article continues:
Starts during the seven months of 1949 totalled 49,285 compared with 49,452 in the first seven months of 1948.

National Housing Act
According to these figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics, there were less houses started this year than last year. 1 understood the minister to say that more houses were started this year than last year, so there must be something wrong. The figures I have quoted were released by the dominion bureau of statistics. Certainly, it is evident that the rate at which houses are being built is not meeting our requirements. Some different measures, therefore, will have to be taken if we are to overcome that lag.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I think one of the most urgent needs in Canada today is a program which will supply low-rental housing. No matter how many houses we may build for those who have sufficient money to construct them under private enterprise, no matter how many of those houses we may build for those who can take advantage of the National Housing Act, it still will not meet the requirements of people who have not the money to build a house. This is particularly true of the labouring class. These people just have not enough money to lay aside a portion of their monthly income to make the required down payment. It does not matter how small that down payment is.
As the member who preceded me said, people cannot afford to spend more than one-fifth of their income for rent. That being so, the greatest need is for low-rental housing. Labouring people, and many so-called white collar employees, are in positions which do not lend themselves to the owing of a house. Some of these people are apt to be transferred from one position to another, yet they have not a sufficient income to pay the exorbitant rents which are being asked today. The other day I pointed out that there are thousands of people in this country, and in my own city particularly, that are receiving from $100 to $135 per month. It is exceedingly difficult to lay aside sufficient from that salary to pay rentals of anywhere from $40 to $70 per month. Many of these people cannot afford to pay anything in excess of $20 per month for rent.
This is the problem with which we are faced today, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me inevitable that this government will have to have a program of subsidized low-rental housing. The problem cannot be solved through any financial corporation. It must be done through the government, if we are to give the people who so urgently need it low-rental housing.
Let me speak for a moment about the cost of housing. When it comes to dealing with those people who are taking advantage of the National Housing Act, then of course the cost of the house is a material consideration. One of the factors which contribute to the high

cost of building a house under the national housing plan is the rate of interest that must be paid. I have always maintained that 4J per cent or 5 per cent is entirely too much. As I said on one other occasion last year, it seems to me that the government is now endeavouring to provide a field of investment for financial institutions instead of building low-cost houses. During the war and since that time I have oftened wondered where the mortgage companies would have received anything approaching 41, per cent for their money if the government had not initiated this housing program. There is no other field in which these loan companies could have invested their money so safely.
This is particularly true when one considers that the government guarantees their losses to the extent of 25 per cent. It seems to me a safe investment for the mortgage companies, because they take absolutely no risk that I can see. They take no responsibility for the construction of the house. The onus is entirely on the purchaser, and it is so stated in the contract. If the purchaser fails to make one payment on time, his whole equity may be entirely washed out.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that on another occasion I had the contracts here in the house. When I raised the question at that time, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. He pointed out to me how absurd it was for me to suggest that these loan companies would be so inhuman as to throw people out of their homes and destroy their equity. At that time I said that it was not whether they would or would not do it, but there was a provision in the contract which enabled the loan companies to wipe out every cent the purchaser had put into the house. That very thing did come to pass. Veterans in Calgary who built under the N.H.A. lost every cent they had put in those houses, owing entirely to the mortgage company's foreclosing on them because they had not made payments, and for other reasons. I believe that one of the greatest contributions the minister could make to prospective builders would be to see that these contracts are redrawn so that the man who purchases a house under the National Housing Act will be guaranteed his equity in that property.
One large item of cost which enters into the building of a house is the interest charges. I am entirely in accord with those who suggest that the interest rates under the National Housing Act should be cut down. Surely, an insurance company should not be given any greater interest rate on its investment than the ordinary person who is trying

to provide for comfort in his old age by buying an annuity. The government saw fit to reduce the rates on annuities from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. If it was fair to do that, surely it is just as fair to reduce these interest rates from 4J per cent to 3 per cent.
The minister said, I think-though I am just speaking from recollection now-that the cost of materials was down about 1 per cent and that wages were up about 3 per cent. I do not know where he got his information in that regard. The cost of building a house today definitely is 50 per cent higher than it was right after the war. I know that from an actual experience of my own. For the house that I built four years ago, the lumber alone would cost me $3,500 more now; or rather, a year ago it would have cost me that; it would cost even more than that now. The lumberman who supplied the lumber gave me that quotation. That is a tremendous increase in the cost of lumber alone. I have yet to see any lumber yards with which I have ever done business going broke.
But that cost is not nearly so bad as the tremendous interest rates which these people are asked to pay on their loans. It may be true that wages have increased; in fact, it is true. There is no doubt about that. That too would add to the costs. But I believe the government could render a service to the people of Canada if they would take such steps as are necessary to see to it that the costs of building materials are reduced.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, when I was going through the United States on my way home- we have not a Canadian highway on which we can travel; we must go through the United States; when he gets the houses built, perhaps the minister will give us a highway -I made it my business to check on the cost of some of the building materials. I found that, even on the west coast, where prices are higher than they are in the central part of the United States, lumber was cheaper there than it was in western Canada. I found that plumbing equipment was cheaper there than it is here, as was hardware. It seems to me that there is quite a field there which might be advantageously investigated, and that the result might be worth-while savings in the construction of these houses.
Let me speak of one other thing which the minister mentioned, namely, the price of ;hese houses, and particularly the end price. When the minister was speaking on Septem-rer 21, as reported at page 119 of Hansard, re had this to say:
It is proposed that the present level of loans to louse builders would be little changed.
Then on a little further:
There would be no restrictions upon the builder is to the price at which he may sell the house.
National Housing Act
In my view that is wrong. The minister of course will say to me: If we are going to give a loan on a house, then the price must be fair and reasonable; and this morning I think he gave the formula on which that fair and reasonable price would be determined. But in my judgment that is not enough. I do not see how this government can loan money to contractors building houses and then permit them to sell those houses at any price they like. To me that just does not seem to be good business. But I take it that is exactly what will happen under this plan. I believe that there should be some control on the selling price of the house.
The government of course may be trying to get out from under something which they have experienced in the past.
In answer to one of the questions put to him, the minister repeated what he had said on many other occasions, namely that there was no contract between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the lending institution and the builder. I disagree with that statement, and I hope that some of the courts will disagree with it. Without question, there is an agreement. You can call it an agreement, a contract or anything you like. There is an agreement between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the lending institution and the builder. Whether you call it an agreement or a contract is a matter of quibbling, I think. Under that agreement certain standards of buildings are set up. Specifications must be submitted, and a plan must be submitted for the approval of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If that does not constitute a contract, I do not know what does. There you have the type of house determined, and you have the plans and specifications submitted. They must meet the approval of the institution. If that is so-and I take it that it is so, because I have seen the agreement-surely the government must have some say as to the selling price of that house.
The minister went on to say a while ago that it was not the cost that mattered but that it was the selling price. Then we must take into consideration the selling price; and if the government, through the lending institution, is going to make building loans to these builders building for sale, then certainly there must be some control on the selling price of that house. Suppose that a fair and reasonable price for a house is, we will say, $8,000. Are we going to allow them to sell that house for $12,000 or $14,000 to people who are desirous of buying it and who of necessity must buy a house? If we are trying to solve our housing problem, are we going to allow these men whom the government finances through the lending institutions to hold up the public who are in such great need of these houses? It

National Housing Act
just does not sound sensible. My view therefore is that there must be some control over the selling prices of these houses of the type of which I was just speaking.
In my remarks today I am endeavouring to give the house some suggestions whereby I think our building program can be improved.
I want to say something about the qualifications of the builder. I do so because experience has taught us that the greatest difficulty the housing program has ever got into was because of some of the things I am about to mention now, and have mentioned in the past. One of them is the soundness of the construction. I have told the minister this privately,
I tell it to him here, and I have mentioned it in the house before. I think one of the greatest difficulties the government has found itself in was not through their building program exactly but rather through the inefficiency and incompetence of the inspectors employed by them. On almost every occasion I can think of I could trace the difficulty back to inefficient inspection. In the little pamphlet which the government puts out, it is true that they speak about sound standards of construction, and about the specifications and so on. An outline is given in the book which the government sends out, or which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation sends out to the public, called "The Integrated Housing Plan", which is distributed all over the country. The people who get that book have confidence that the houses that are going to be built will be of sound construction.
That is not just so. They are fooled again, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat points out. Certainly if the buildings were constructed according to plans and specifications they would be of sound construction. The point arises however that the man whom the government has as its inspector has never seen to it that the plans and specifications were followed. In a great number of cases the specifications of the house have changed entirely without the knowledge of the purchaser, although such purchaser must assume all the responsibility together with the mortgage; that is, according to the government. There should be some different arrangement in that regard.
When the government is letting these agreements they should investigate the contractor to see whether or not he has had building experience sufficient to carry on an enterprise of that kind. Then they should review his financial position to see whether or not he is financially capable of carrying on that portion of the construction for which he is responsible, until he receives his progress payments.
There again the government has failed. These are things upon which the minister

might check so as to save the government and the people who purchase these houses thousands upon thousands of dollars. Right now I can point to at least four large companies which have failed because they did not have sufficient financial backing to carry on construction to the point where they were entitled to progress payments, and for that reason had to fall down on their contracts.
In almost all those cases, however, the government reports-and I could read the statements if I were asked to do so-stated in effect that the financial standing was to the satisfaction of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the lending institution, which is just so much bunk. In the case of the Pelmo construction company at Toronto this fact was evident, as it was also in connection with the Bow River Construction Company at Calgary, where it was even more evident. These companies did not have the financial backing sufficient to carry them up to that stage where they would receive progress payments.
This condition could be easily overcome. One hon. member said to me the other day that if I got too strict in this connection I would have no one building. Well, I would rather not have that type of man building for me. Surely we do not want that kind of contractor building houses for the government or for anyone else. The government has fallen down most miserably in checking the financial condition of some of these people who have been building houses. This is a condition that could be overcome.
In almost every one of the cases concerning which I have had correspondence with the government on the point as to whether the contractors had the contracting ability and the building experience necessary, the same old answer was given, that it has been found to the satisfaction of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that they had that ability. In some of the cases where Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had given approval the organizations concerned had absolutely no building experience.
I believe it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), when he was minister of reconstruction and supply, who said it was the practice that these fellows could sublet to others who did know something about the business. What a lot of silliness! One might as well say he would let a contract to anyone who comes along, so that that person could sublet it to somebody with the necessary building qualifications who would complete the job. Here again is a place where the government could save the country hundreds of thousands of dollars, and I hope this matter will be taken into consideration.

There have been so many building failures involving such large amounts that it seems to me the request I made the other day for a royal commission to investigate such failures is now more warranted than ever. I am not saying this in any spirit of bitterness toward the government. I do say however that when a government crown corporation is handling millions upon millions of dollars there should be some check upon the way in which that money is spent. There should be a check by the House of Commons, if not by a royal commission. A committee of the house should be set up, if the minister is opposed to the appointment of the royal commission I have suggested, before which members of the house could satisfy themselves as to the methods employed in the building and financing of these housing projects.
I do not intend to speak longer. I have many other points in mind, but I believe they may be more properly discussed when the bill is in committee.

Before the debate proceeds further I feel I should make a ruling on the amendment now proposed. In accordance with the custom established, perhaps I should first hear representations either for or against ;he amendment-and in doing so I suggest that such representations be as brief as possible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word in support of the contention that the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) is in order. I shall heed your admonition to be brief, but before proceeding with what I have to say concerning the amendment I believe it would be in order for me to say, on behalf of members on all sides of the house, that we deeply appreciate the manner in which Your Honour is handling these points of order. This offer to hear representations before you rule is really something for which we are most grateful, and in my view it is one of the highlights of this parliament.
The fundamental basis for an amendment of this kind is found in citation 657, Beau-chesne's third edition, which states:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress-
I shall stop there, because the rest does not apply. My contention is that this is an amendment drafted according to the terms of that citation which, for reasons stated in the resolution and for reasons stated in my colleague's speech, expresses opposition to the further progress of this measure until some-
National Housing Act
thing else has been done. That "something else" is a request that the government consider rescinding the order of November 3 which made provision for an increase in domestic rents.
The form as set out in Beauchesne's third edition for this kind of amendment is form No. 93 at page 337. There are in fact several variations of it. They have been more or less put together in the present amendment, but I draw Your Honour's attention particularly to the form which says that:
The further consideration of this bill be deferred until . . .
Such and such had been done.
My colleague asks that second reading of this bill should not now be given. He asks instead that there be prior consideration to the rescinding of the order with respect to rent control. Therefore I suggest that it is carrying out what is provided for in citation 657, and also what is provided for in form 93, which indicates that one can ask that second reading be deferred until something else has been done.
Incidentally the passing of this motion would not kill the bill. It would merely delay its progress, as is clearly set out in May's thirteenth edition. I will not take the time to read it to the house because I do not think there is any doubt on that point so far as Your Honour is concerned. I refer to pages 390, 391 and 392 of May's thirteenth edition.
It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that the only question that might be raised would be whether or not the question in this amendment is relevant to the question involved in the bill before the house. The bill deals with housing, and surely rents are germane to housing. Surely no one can say that rents are foreign to housing, to use a word that appears in one citation. In fact, in introducing the bill the minister had to speak of rents repeatedly. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) did likewise. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) did the same and so did the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) who has just spoken.
The bill proposes to deal with the rental situation in a certain way. My hon. friend and colleague contends that before it is dealt with in that way it should be dealt with in this way, namely by rescinding the order increasing rents.
I also draw your attention to the heading of a ruling made by Mr. Speaker Sutherland on December 10, 1906. It is found on page 576 of Beauchesne's third edition, and reads as follows:
An amendment is relevant when it deals with the same subject-matter as the main motion.

National Housing Act
Certainly part of the subject matter of the main motion has to do with rents. The amendment deals with that part of the main question, and I submit for Your Honour's consideration that it is relevant.

First of all, I wish to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his reference to the way in which I have been giving my rulings and on the custom that has been adopted whereby I am prepared to hear hon. members before I make my rulings. I must say that I intend to continue to do that and I hope that other hon. members will be as brief as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was in this instance.
The amendment before the house at this time proposes to amend the motion that the bill under consideration be now read a second time. The form of the amendment is that the bill be not now read a second time but that the government should give immediate and prior consideration to a certain rentals order. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has referred me to citation 657 of Beauchesne's third edition, which reads:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution;
I do not think the amendment would come within the provisions of the section of that citation as far as I have read them. The citation goes on:
-or otherwise opposed to its progress.
The amendment, being in the proper form, might possibly come within these words. However, I would point out to hon. members that the amendment must be relevant to the question which is under consideration. This amendment suggests that the government give immediate and prior consideration to rescinding an order announced on November 3, providing for increases in domestic rents. May I inform the hon. member that that increase in no way affects any houses that are to be built under this bill. The order with regard to rents affected houses which were in existence in 1941 and probably some time subsequent to that date; but in no way can it be considered that the order affects anything that might be done under this bill. I would refer hon. members to citation 354 of Beauchesne's third edition, which reads as follows:
An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved. (Can. C. J. Vol. LX, p. 122.)

In my opinion this amendment deals with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the motion which is now before the house, and is therefore not relevant, and I must accordingly rule it out of order.

Mr. Speaker, my first words are words of congratulation and commendation to the minister on the most heartening statement of government policy which he made early today. In the course of his remarks I was particularly impressed when he pointed out that in 1946 we set before us housing objectives, and that in 1949 we had fully achieved them and realized them. That for me holds out considerable hope for the bill we have now before us.
In 1946 we said that we would do certain things. We come back here in 1949 and we say that we did them. Now we set ourselves an entirely new objective in this bill, and I am satisfied that once again we shall be able to come back to this house and to the country and say that we accomplished exactly what we set out to do.
Some time ago an hon. member informed this house that during the last campaign I had more to say about housing, as he put it, than any other hon. member. Let me just read what I did say about housing during the campaign. I think the house will be interested in that. I shall quote from the Toronto Star of May 4:
David Croll, Liberal M.P. for Spadina, predicted last night that, shortly after the federal election, the Liberal government will announce a sweeping program of low-rental housing, because experience has shown private enterprise has failed to solve the problem of housing, which the speaker described as "a social problem, a great national emergency."
According to the Toronto Star of June 13, I said:
In the light of present conditions, the government must undertake, in co-operation with the provincial and municipal authorities, to build low-cost rental and subsidized housing.
On July 6, at a meeting held in the office of the mayor of Toronto, at which I was present, along with other hon. members of parliament, I had this to say, as reported in the Globe and Mail of that date:
Let there be no question as to the government's position in this respect.
I was dealing with housing.
We intend to carry out our campaign promises in connection with low-rental housing.
While I am on the subject, I think it presents me with a good opportunity to set the record straight as to what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said about housing. I do so in order to give the house the benefit of his remarks, and the oppor-

tunity to appreciate the evolution of a Liberal mind. In October of 1947 he was quoted as having said:
No government of which I am a member would ever pass legislation for subsidized housing.
This statement has been quoted in the house time and time again by members of the opposition to the point where I firmly believe that they would have preferred him not to change his mind. That is the way they would have liked to have his mind remain. Later on, when he became Prime Minister, he came to Toronto, and he is quoted in the Toronto Star of February 19, 1948, as having said, speaking of housing:
That does not mean that we do not recognize the need for housing units at low rents. With today's costs, it must be obvious that low-rental housing cannot be provided without some kind of financial assistance. Our legislation provides for slum clearance grants, and also for loans to limited dividend companies for the construction of low-rental housing. It may be that experience will show that other forms of federal assistance will be desirable.
Then we have the Liberal manifesto issued in Moncton on May 20, in which he said:
We are not going to be satisfied until decent housing is provided for every family. All levels of government must combine to promote low-rental housing projects, slum clearance and community planning.
Then we come to what the Prime Minister said at Stratford, Ontario, on June 4. The report in the Toronto Star of that date reads in part as follows:
"We should not rest until every Canadian has a decent home to live in." He stressed that housing is not a federal responsibility. "But we have said that if any province or any other governing body will come to us with a proposition, it will find that the federal government is ready to share with it the responsibility and expense of providing houses."
Then on June 8 at the city of Quebec the Prime Minister said:
For many people low-rental housing is essential... Municipal and provincial authorities obviously have to decide what is feasible and desirable before we can give effective help. But I certainly feel strongly that we in Canada should push ahead vigorously with our housing policy because more and better housing raises the standard of living; low-rental housing promotes improved health and greater social and family security for those with low incomes; and an active housing program helps to keep up employment in the construction industry which, as you know so well, is one of our least stable industries. A successful housing program depends upon good town and community planning. Increased cost, and complexity of governmental action in the development of towns and cities, emphasizes the importance of careful long term planning to avoid needless expenditure.
Today we have this bill before us, to amend the National Housing Act, and naturally I am happy to endorse it because the National Housing Act has become a landmark in Canadian history. Over the years it has made it
National Housing Act
possible for many people to become home owners who otherwise might not have been able to do so. At the present time we find that the country from Halifax to Vancouver is dotted with N.H.A. homes. To that extent it has become a part of our Canadian way of life. The proposal today is to broaden the application of the act and when the amendments before us are adopted it will make it a truly national housing act. The present amendments make it more than ever a bill with a purpose, and the purpose is to create more and better housing for all the people of Canada.
If this bill means anything at all, it means public housing; it means low-rental housing; it means subsidized housing. I should like to quote now from the Ottawa Journal of November 12. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) addressed the Dominion United Church men's association, and the newspaper report reads in part:
He said that the principle had been admitted that homes in low economy areas must be subsidized, and added that the work of clearing slum sections was important.
Furthermore, for the information of those who may not have caught the full import of the statement he made today, I should like to point out that he said:
The project, however,-
Speaking of dominion-provincial house building.
-will remain in ownership of the dominion and the province. The operating profit or loss will be borne 75 per cent by the dominion and 25 per cent by the province.
These are important words.
The annual subsidy will be the amount by which rentals received are less than operating costs of all kinds, including depreciation. These operating losses will be met on an annual basis 75 per cent by the dominion and 25 per cent by the province.
How much clearer could anyone be than in that particular statement? I think we have sufficient background so that we can now discuss the bill and the principle involved in it. The amendments bring to the act a principle that, in my opinion, is of the greatest social significance. I think the house and the country should recognize it exactly for what it is. Today for the first time we are asked to accept the proposition that housing is a social as well as an economic problem. I gladly accept it as do my fellow members on this side of the house. I call upon the rest of the house to join me in hailing this as another forward step in our political and social maturity.
I think the amendment does something even more than that. Here for the first time we have an admission by this or any other

National Housing Act
government of responsibility for housing the nation. We have now taken the initiative, and we must see that we keep it. I need not recall to the house that under our constitution housing is normally a provincial and municipal matter. That has been largely the reason why there has been a failure to solve the housing problem decisively. Each government authority looked to the other two governmental authorities to do something about it with the result that nothing very much was done. As a result housing, because of the differences of opinion, was lost in the zone of non-co-operation which lay between the governmental authorities. The present amendments end an era of indecisiveness. There is no longer a twilight zone. The field has been completely covered, 75 per cent by the dominion government and 25 per cent by the provincial government.
The amendments also do something else. They end once and for all, I hope, the "after you" philosophy which has dogged Canadian housing for many years. They show clearly that the dominion is now prepared to act co-operatively, according to the terms laid down, with all levels of government to provide housing for Canadians who need it. This seems to me to be a great challenge to the people of Canada, and I am sure it is a challenge that they will take up. It is a challenge that gives comfort to all those of us who believe in public housing. One of the important features of the bill is that in order for it to be a success the people will have to interest themselves in the problem. This is a public level project.
I think it should be admitted to begin with that this is not a perfect bill. It is a new field, and inevitably deficiencies will become apparent which we will have to remedy in the light of experience and with the passing of time. But I want to recall to hon. members that all our social legislation, from old age pensions to family allowances, has been amended and improved with the passing of time and the gaining of experience; and this housing legislation will prove to be no exception. Imperfect it may be, though I do not suggest that at all; yet it is a very fine beginning. It is important, too, that the government has not placed a price tag on housing, and has not attempted to deal with this question in pennies. At the present time under this legislation we are allocating some $50 million. That is a nice beginning. It will cost more, and hon. members must expect that, as I am sure the country will. Today we are making a capital investment in human welfare; and when a government does that it is money well spent.
This government is saying to the provinces and municipalities: this is what we propose to do. We are partners, and we will share the load on the basis of 75 per cent for the dominion and 25 per cent for the province. We will increase our assistance to the builders, subject to one special safeguard, that of a fair and reasonable selling price. That point has occasioned some comment by other hon. members. It may not appear important to some, but those of us who had some intimate association with wartime housing following the first war will know that it is a guarantee of protection for the home owner. Certainly we could not be forgiven if twice in one generation we made the same mistake, and this provision is an attempt to prevent that happening.
Finally the dominion is saying this: we will enter into agreements with provinces to build publicly assisted housing, including low rental housing on an economic or subsidized basis. There, Mr. Speaker, you have it. For the first time, in speaking of housing, it is safe to use the word "subsidized" without being considered a wild-eyed radical. It has taken a long time; but when the need was fairly placed before the government they did not hesitate to take action. So at long last the government, to its everlasting credit, has taken a direct stand in the field of subsidized housing, something that will be hailed from one end of this country to the other as one of the most progressive and far-reaching measures ever introduced in this house, in my opinion comparable to the family allowance legislation. This 21st parliament has much to commend it. So far it has dealt with two constitutional problems of great importance; yet I venture to predict that long after those have come to be taken for granted this parliament will be remembered for this legislation which at last recognizes housing as a matter of social welfare and a problem of national concern.
I know our opponents are criticizing this legislation. That is the function of an opposition. Already from the right we have suggestions that we are giving too much, while on the left they are saying we are not giving enough. Well, that was ever the way, as we well know. However, I prefer to welcome this bill for what it is, a very long step forward in government thinking. And believe me, the step was not taken any too soon. Today, as has been pointed out, the need for housing is immediate and urgent, and in some instances almost tragic. We cannot deny that lately it has become aggravated. That is particularly true in the low-income groups, whose rate of family increase is

greatest and whose ability to pay is the smallest. We have now reached the point where we cannot let any more grass grow under our feet. We need action, and we need it quickly. We need to pass, proclaim, plan and put up houses, even before spring is here, because time is working against us. We have a backlog now of nearly 500,000 units which are badly needed; and the need increases daily as our population increases and our present housing units become more obsolete.
This amendment, of course, is not aimed primarily at the upper bracket Canadians. They have always been able to look after themselves. They have always been able to build or buy houses. No doubt this legislation will help them, but the amendment is not intended for their specific benefit. They do not constitute the real social problem with which we have to deal in this country. The problem is posed to us by that one-third of our nation who cannot afford to buy or rent homes constructed by private builders at present costs. The latest figures I can find from the taxation department, which I believe are for 1947, show that one and a quarter million taxpayers in Canada had incomes of $2,000 or less. Well, from there on it is a matter of simple arithmetic, the kind every head of a family sits up nights working out but hardly ever solves. The top figure of $2,000 a year means an income of $166 per month. We are told that an economic rent is somewhere between 20 and 23 per cent of the monthly income. This means that our Canadian earning that top income of $2,000 a year can afford to pay only $38 a month in rent; and it must be remembered that $2,000 a year is the ceiling. Some of the one and a quarter million taxpayers earn much less than that. So it has long been clear that those earning $25 to $40 a week cannot possibly obtain adequate housing accommodation at today's costs. They must be helped.
The answer is subsidized housing. In this bill the government has recognized a very important principle. The real issue in housing is no longer materials or manpower; it is cost. No housing plan is going to relieve the present shortage unless something is done to reduce the cost to the occupant, whether he be owner or tenant. Over the years the National Housing Act has helped thousands of Canadians to own their own homes. In the first seven months of 1948 more than
11,000	Canadians took advantage of that legislation. It is true that by lowering the down payment the act increases the number of potential owners, and by extending the
National Housing Act
amortization period it makes it easier for others to obtain houses at a more reasonable rental. But neither of these affects the cost. The longer amortization, good as it is, merely spreads today's inflated building costs over a longer period of years. It is true that it makes housing more easily available to those who can afford it, but what about the one-third of the nation which cannot afford to pay even the smallest down payment, or which cannot afford to carry even the present generous amortization plan. These are the people who need assistance immediately. These are the people who need subsidized housing now. It is for that reason I say to the minister, we have no time .to lose.
Now that we have taken the wraps off this terrible and terrifying word "subsidized", we look around and notice some rather surprising things. One is that we have been in the subsidizing business for some considerable length of time. Fourteen per cent of the building completed in 1949 was subsidized by this government. This government has already built 50,000 subsidized houses for veterans, both low-cost and low-rental houses. No one will say that veterans housing has not been a tremendous success. We have already proven to the country that subsidized housing is workable and beneficial.
Under the principle contained in this bill, it will be possible to do something for the rest of the Canadian people who need homes in the very same way. If we can build 50,000 subsidized homes, we can build 100,000 subsidized homes. We can build as many as this country needs, as many as this country asks for, or as many as this country can digest. One thing we must not forget, the initial drive must now come from the municipalities. Low-rental and subsidized housing must have grass roots enthusiasm emanating from the cities and towns in which the houses will be built. What we are setting up by this act is the machinery for housing the nation.
Writing a cheque, in itself, is not good enough and the minister fully recognizes that. It is not enough for us to write a cheque and say to the provinces or municipalities, "There you are, you have the money, it is your baby; you bring it up." By this act housing becomes our baby from this time forward. We have to see to it that it becomes a full grown, healthy adult. The dominion is providing for 75 per cent of the cost and 25 per cent will be borne by the province. Profits and losses are to be divided on the same basis. In a broad scheme such as this, there will be losses. They are inevitable if we are to have the full benefit of subsidized houses.

National Housing Act
In'addition to that, the dominion government provides the research knowledge, technical and administrative experience, and the provincial government provides the local knowledge and considerable experience. The municipalities provide two things which will cost them nothing. They provide the initiative and the local services. The services are to be paid for by normal taxes. There will be no cost to the municipalities. The subsidy which in the past the municipalities gave to wartime housing now comes to an end. It is expected that the municipalities will provide serviced land, either immediately or whenever it is required of them. They will be repaid every cent of the cost for providing the land, in the same way that any taxpayer pays his taxes.
We only ask one more thing from the municipalities, and that is that they do some intelligent planning. Public housing cannot be like Topsy, it cannot just grow. It must be planned systematically, carefully and intelligently. I believe the importance of planning becomes all too evident when one looks around and sees the result of unplanned private building. I am thinking of areas around the city of Toronto, but it is applicable to Ottawa, Windsor and practically every municipality across this country. One finds row upon row of homes, identical bungalows. It must be a nightmare for someone coming home on Saturday night. They are crowded together as closely as possible with a minimum of air, light and recreational space. Many private builders, and the government to some extent, seem to forget that houses are meant to be lived in by human beings. There is more to housing than four walls and a roof.
The public housing which this act envisages must be built intelligently and with great imagination. There must be planning. Little communities will be growing up here and there. They must have lots of green spaces, schools, stores and recreational facilities. The aim cannot be to squeeze in as many low cost houses as possible into a given area of land. It must be to provide a pattern of living by means of which people may lead happier, healthier lives. That is what I meant, Mr. Speaker, when I said that housing is now a social as well as economic problem.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Not just now, no.

Will you permit a question later?
I am convinced that we can house this nation, provided we obtain the co-operation

of the provinces and the municipalities. I commend the minister now for the trip he took across this country earlier this year, when he visited the premiers and the men responsible for housing in the various provinces. He came back with an agreement. I am suggesting to the minister that he take another one of those Winters travels across this country immediately after the passage of this bill, for the purpose of implementing the intention of the house.
This act provides the means, but the real drive must now' come from the people in the municipalities. If the people of this country are alive to the unlimited possibilities of this act for human good, if they are vigorous and concerted in their approach, and if the provinces will do their part by co-ordinating and co-operating, this country will have housing as it never had it before. This problem is vital today. The need will, I hope, never be greater and our ability to finance the program is beyond question.
Bad and inadequate housing has been the worst blemish on our generation. Crime, social unrest, lowered health standards and human waste, have all stemmed from bad housing conditions. To some extent all these conditions can be ameliorated, if not eliminated, by an adequate level of housing. We come down to this: that adequate housing is an integral part of the welfare state we are building in Canada. This is a great contribution to it. Like education and good health, it must not be reserved for the few who can afford to pay for it. Like education and good health, it must be made available to all people who need it.
I believe that the Canadian people are solidly behind this venture. Already there is a wide cross-section of public opinion which has fully endorsed subsidized housing. Let me relate a few.
It has been endorsed by the Canadian Legion, by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, by welfare and social councils across Canada, by the Canadian Congress of Labour, by the American Federation of Labor, and by church groups, by the Canadian Construction Association and by socially minded people across this country. But they must do something more than merely endorse. They must actively press their municipal authorities to take full advantage of this act. It is impossible, and it would be undesirable, for us here to impose housing on the Canadian people. There must be a desire and a demand, which I am certain are there, which will make themselves not only heard but felt at the municipal and provincial

levels. The Canadian people can rest assured of one thing, that the dominion will do its part.
Such, then, is our new housing act which is reaching out to new horizons. The only people who stand to lose by this act are the slum owners and shelter profiteers. The country stands to gain. This act will assist many Canadians to own their own homes and will assist others to rent decent, adequate housing at prices that they can afford to pay. I think this act, if fully implemented will eliminate soft spots in our economy and will keep our way of life secure. I know that this will cost money; but no matter what it costs, it will be cheap in comparison with the good that it will do. I think that this is an excellent beginning.
Just one more word of urgency. In the light of other decisions which we have made, this act at the present time should have the highest priority with the minister. We must hurry, hurry, hurry and get building done as quickly as we possibly can. I do not expect the minister to go out and lay bricks; but anything short of that I am prepared to accept. We must not forget this fact. When we endorse the principle of this bill, we accept responsibility, and then we must follow through. We have already paid too high a price for slowness in this country.
I heartily endorse the principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker. I congratulate the minister and the government, and I am happy to find myself in support of a government that sponsors a bill such as this.

My brief remarks this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, will I believe reflect in the main the opinions held by the majority of the people of the riding that I represent in this house.
First, I should like to compliment the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) and the government for realizing that, in spite of the extensive housing program across the nation, the need for housing with all its accompanying difficulties continues to be one of Canada's most serious problems. In fact, in many of our larger centres the need for housing seems as great as ever.
While I realize our responsibility in this most urgent matter, however, I feel obliged to offer a word of caution in respect of the rental phase of our assistance as proposed by this bill. As all hon. members know, the most acute need for housing exists in those areas in which we have a density of population caused by industrial expansion. Does it not seem reasonable that the industries and the municipalities causing this influx of population and, of course, benefiting from it, should share the costs and the responsibility in this regard? To me it does not seem fair that, in this country in which so many of our people live on farms and in small towns, this section of our people should be penalized and forced to subsidize certain urban dwellers. Furthermore, such action can only accelerate the movement of our people from the farm and the small towns and cities and further defeat the plans and hopes of those of us who believe, for various reasons, that industry should be decentralized across this nation.
As I said at the beginning, I am glad our government realizes the need for housing and is doing something about it; but I urge that we proceed cautiously in this rental phase of our proposed assistance. As for the rest of the bill-that is, with the portion of the bill to assist home ownership-I am thoroughly in accord with it. I have the good fortune to live in North Bay where we boast a high percentage of home owners; in fact, 75 per cent of our homes are owner-occupied. This home ownership, I believe, is the greatest single factor in the general well-being and stability of our people. The

National Housing Act
urge to own one's own home is strong in the hearts of Canadians; and this portion of the bill is designed further to develop and stimulate this urge to the end that it may become a reality.
I do not believe many Canadians want to live in subsidized homes with another section of our population being penalized. What the majority of Canadians want is an opportunity to own their own homes. I urge the minister to make this section of the bill as workable as possible. Let us cut those down payments to a minimum, so that they will be within reach of all our people. When I say "all our people" I mean just that. I do not subscribe to the theory that a large portion of the Canadian people are incapable of owning their own property, nor do I share the view that certain people are doomed to live in subsidized rental accommodation for the rest of their days.
Further, when this legislation becomes effective, I would urge that special attention be given to publicizing these amendments to the National Housing Act through every possible means-in other words, let us popularize this N.H.A. plan-so that we may hasten the day when as many of our people as possible may own their own homes.
I have just one further observation to make. I would urge on the minister, in the application of these new amendments, that everything possible be done to encourage the building of small low-cost homes. I know the minister has this in mind, but I think it warrants serious consideration; because the low-cost home of today in terms of our present-day thinking is, in fact, the high-priced home of a few years ago. I need scarcely remind hon. members of the days when our economy was not so buoyant, of the days when our people who had purchased high-priced homes during a previous period of economic buoyancy were being hard pressed to meet their obligations and when, as you know, thousands of homes were lost, along with every dollar the owner had invested.
I am not suggesting that we are headed for another period like the early 30's; but at the same time, one would be foolish to plan his future on the assumption that our present high level of prosperity will continue to climb unabated. The point I want to make, sir, is this. As I move around this country today I see young inexperienced people buying high-priced homes, little realizing the seriousness of their obligations, of the crushing burden of interest payments, instalments on principal, local taxes, insurance, maintenance. Let us not be responsible for saddling our people with homes that in the future will be monuments to debt and misery,

but rather let us especially encourage low-priced small homes where our young people can meet their obligations and still enjoy al least some of the luxuries of life.
If and when these small homes are partially or fully paid for, they can be resold to othei young people starting out in life and the former owner with his increased equity can then step into a higher-priced home that will be more in keeping with his more mature requirements and capabilities.
