These totals mean nothing when compared with the need for better homes in rural Canada. The failure of the government to interest any large corporation or manufacturer in the production of suitable bathroom units and toilet facilities for rural homes is deplorable. From 1944 to the present time we find the government has been able to interest only one manufacturer, and him only in a tentative way-he has not yet even made an application-for the production of these facilities. Goodness knows they are needed in rural Canada.
I have not the statistics with me, but I did place on record during the last parliament figures which showed that approximately 90 per cent of homes in urban areas have running water and bathroom facilities whereas 90 per cent of rural homes have neither. Surely there is something lacking in a country like Canada where in rural districts the homes of the greatest single wealth-producing group in the country are of this kind.
National Housing Act
That is the one blind spot in the minister's legislation. Something should be done to rectify the condition and to meet the need for better homes in rural Canada. I hope some other members representing rural areas will add their voices in urging the government to meet this need.

Wherever you go in Canada today you find the strongest possible evidence of the fact that we are enjoying the greatest building boom that this country has ever had. You do not need to go to the bureau of statistics to satisfy yourself as to that. Your own eyes are sufficient evidence of the fact. All types of building, not only homes but all types of construction, factories, stores, churches,

National Housing Act
schools and so forth, all types of building that you can think of are being erected. In my own community I have never seen anything like the building activity which we have today. If hon. members will glance at the statement that I have put on record they will notice that the total of all building construction in Canada in the year 1939 was $159 million odd. By 1947 our total building construction had moved up to $838 million. Complete figures are not yet available for 1948 and 1949, but I am reliably informed that our total building construction this year will run well over a billion dollars. Compare that figure with $159 million in 1939.
Coming to residential construction, the total value of house building in 1939 was just over $53 million. By 1947 we had moved up to $320 million, and this year we shall go well over $400 million. There will be that many dollars' worth of houses built in the one year. If hon. members will check over the housing units they will find that in the years prior to the war our peak year was 1939 when we built 42,000 new houses. By the end of this year the minister estimates we shall have built 96,000 new housing units. Expressed in other words, we have geared up the building trades of this country, so far as house building is concerned, to over double the number of houses which we built in 1939, which was our normal production of houses prior to the war.
I should like to remind the house that this remarkable achievement in house building has been accomplished notwithstanding the heaviest competition, competition in other branches of building. If hon. members will check over the table again they will see that in this year, in addition to the tremendous house building program, we shall have built over $600 million worth of stores, factories, schools, institutions and the like. We all know that the change-over from wartime production to peacetime production is a difficult one. Because of that, in the early years after the war we ran into many bottlenecks in the building trades. Plumbing fixtures, soil pipe, electrical supplies, seasoned lumber, doors, hardwood flooring, nails, cement, brick, gyproc, fibreboard and countless other items I could mention were all in short supply. Most of them are becoming easier today, but cement, bricks and nails are still in short supply.
Since the war, and certainly in 1947 and the early part of 1948, the builders of this country spent well over one-third of their time searching for building materials and chasing up the delivery of those materials. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this tremendous expansion in our building trades, this tremendous expansion in house building, did not

come about by mere accident. It came aboul by good planning and able leadership. Toe much credit cannot be paid to the house building trades of this country for the persevering way in which they carried on in 1946, 1947 and 1948 under these constantly recurring bottlenecks of one type of building supplies and the other. They cannot be given too much credit for their ingenuity in improvising and substituting one type of material for another that was in short supply.
Another branch to which some credit is due is our lending institutions. We should express appreciation of our lending institutions for the wonderful way in which they have co-operated and made the finances available for the tremendous program which we have had. I am proud to say that this country owes a deep debt of gratitude to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe! who was responsible for the organization ol this program, and also to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I can only speak of my own community because I know it well, and while I travel to some extent I do not pretend to speak for the rest of Canada. In my own community, so far as housing is concerned, one part of the problem is well under control. I refer to the part that has to do with home ownership. With the assistance which I have mentioned, so far as the private home owner is concerned the problem is well under control and we are making quite good progress.
The remaining hard core of the problem, as I should like to term it, is the need for low-rental housing. In view of the achievements, and in view of all the surrounding circumstances, I was hopeful that there would be some helpful suggestions from the opposition as to how the low-rental problem should be tackled. I also fully expected that we would have some expression of appreciation from the official opposition for what has been accomplished. I was both surprised and disappointed with the speech delivered by the opposition's official housing critic when the bill was up for first reading. On re-reading his speech carefully and going over it from beginning to end, I fail to find any helpful suggestion for the solution of the problem. In addition to that, about the only thing that one can find is a long list of misleading grumbling complaints. May I read a few of them to the house. At page 1297 of Hansard the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) said:
When we look back on these post-war years from 1945 to 1949 Inclusive, we can say that so far as housing is concerned they will go down as the wasted years.
Further down on the same page there are these words:
The record during the past five years has been a record of failure . . .
Over on the next page I find these words:
Progress by this government in three precious years in spite of all this boasting and these promises-absolutely nil!
No progress. I wondered, when I re-read these statements, what on earth the hon. member for Eglinton has been doing with himself. Has he been going around blindfold, or what is the matter with him? In the same speech at page 1302 of Hansard there are more complaints, and I find these words:
I have said before that there has been far too rigid and unsympathetic administration of the National Housing Act.
Again on the same page are these words:
. . . but I do not intend to spare the feelings of the supporters of the government any more than I have been.

Of course they were smug, they were satisfied just as they are today, and they followed the course of just letting the people who were faced with the housing problem worry about it.
I have a suggestion to make to the hon. member for Eglinton. If he will not believe what he sees himself, if he will not believe his own eyes, if he will not believe the material that is available to him in the dominion bureau of statistics and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, then I would ask him to be good enough to go and talk with the son of a former Conservative minister of finance, a lifelong Tory, who will not lead him astray politically. I refer to Mr. Rhodes. I believe at the present time he is president or past president of the Ottawa real estate board. He is a man who has made a wonderful contribution in Ottawa towards the solution of Canada's housing problem. X invite members of the house to go and inspect Mr. Rhodes' Manor Park suburban development. I ask the hon. member for Eglinton to inquire of Mr. Rhodes whether progress in house building since the end of the war has been nil, if they have been wasted years, if it is a record of failure. I also ask him particularly to ask Mr. Rhodes if the administration of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been unsympathetic or smug, and whether the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and this government have let people who were in distress for housing do their own worrying.
They certainly have.

Enough of that. My object in speaking today is to try to sell an idea to the private members of the house. The first thing I wish to do is to urge as strongly as I can that our housing problem is much too vital for anyone to play politics with it. '
Page the government.

In the first place I do not think it is good enough for private members, whether on the government or opposition sides of the house, to content themselves with simply grumbling about it. I suggest to all private members of the house that we should go to work and help in the effort to solve the housing problem in our own ridings. I hope I shall be pardoned if I make a personal reference. As I view it, as I said a moment ago, the remaining hard core of our housing problem is one of rentals. I think there are two distinct groups requiring rental accommodation, and I think they should be kept in two separate compartments as to their needs and the remedy to be applied. The first group

National Housing Act
comprises a limited number, and every community has them. It consists of a few folk who, on account of old age, ill health, or some misfortune of one kind or another, find themselves in a position where they cannot afford to pay the economic rent for decent housing accommodation. Their number is relatively small but their need is most urgent. In Burlington we have these people.
The mayor of the town, Major Leather, and I organized a housing plan for these unfortunates under the existing National : Housing Act. You will find under that act that 90 per cent of the cost at 3 per cent interest is available for this purpose in any municipality, but there are two restrictions. In the first place the sponsors of the scheme, who put up the 10 per cent equity, must be 'content with a 5 per cent interest return on their money. The other restriction is that the housing units constructed under the plan must not be rented to anyone except the needy folk to whom I have referred. The major and I organized such a scheme in my home town. It was sponsored by the Lions Club, the Legion and the town of Burlington. We raised the 10 per cent owner equity as a gift. We did not pay any interest on it. We built the most modern type of units that we could. They are of fireproof masonry construction, and are attractive in appearance. We rent the nicest little housing suites you ever saw at $16 and $21 a month. They have white-tile bathrooms, and nicely equipped kitchens with everything that the heart could desire. The rentals of $16 and $21 a month pay all of the operating costs. By the way, we were able to get an amortization period of forty-seven years on the mortgage, because the buildings were well constructed. Those rentals pay the expenses of the caretaker, the cost of fuel, and all operating costs. What we have done in Burlington has been repeated in one or two other municipalities in Canada, but in far too few; and I suggest to the private members of this house, especially to our critical friends in the opposition, that they get busy in their own ridings and help solve Canada's housing problem in so far as it concerns these unfortunate people.
As to the other part of the problem, the provision of low-rental housing for the workmen of this country, I do not know how many units we need. My guess would be somewhere between one hundred and two hundred thousand housing units. I am pleased indeed that this amendment to the National Housing Act provides for co-operation between governments at all three levels, municipal, provincial and federal, for the solution of this problem. On a question as

important as housing it is not surprising that we should find differences of opinion. I am quite free to admit that I do not find myself in agreement with all hon. members of my own party on this point; nevertheless I want to express my personal views as to how I believe the problem should be tackled. Today in Canada a large percentage of our workmen already own their own homes or are well on the way to ownership. The national advantages which flow from private ownership of homes simply cannot be overestimated. The home owner who has to struggle to pay for his own home has a real stake in the country; and I would very much dislike to see Canada, through a large-scale subsidy program, degenerate into a country of tenants. I do not think we should allow that to happen. I am not unmindful of the fact that a limited amount of rental housing accommodation is essential. Folk move from one community to another; their jobs change, and we must have rental accommodation to take care of that small floating part of our population, if I may so term it.
I was pleased indeed to hear the minister say today that nothing will be done to dull private initiative with respect to home building. I may be reading more into those words than I should, but I hope they mean what I think they do. I hope the minister plans that whatever is done to help solve this housing problem will be done right across the board and that savings in cost effected through land assembly, or savings made in other ways, will be made available not only for the benefit of the man who needs rental accommodation but also for the benefit of the man who wants to and should buy his own home. I would urge that never in this country should we have a subsidy scheme going so far that it would be to the advantage of folk to rent rather than buy, or which would be carried to the point where Canada would eventually become a land of tenants.
Proper planning and financing of the servicing of new land can do much to lower costs; and on this point I have a suggestion to offer the minister. Since the early thirties, when many municipalities in Ontario got into difficulties, our municipal board has been insisting on the repayment of debentures for both water works and sewers over a short period of time. I think fifteen or twenty years is the maximum period for which a debenture issue covering either water or sewers may be approved. We all know that a cast-iron water main in the ground is good for at least sixty to eighty years in most parts of Canada, while a well-laid sanitary sewer has an indefinite life. It would greatly help in bringing down local improvement

payments in taxes if the minister could effect some arrangement under which the payments to defray the cost of sewers and water mains would be spread over a long period of years, rather than the short period which now prevails.
Then, too, I entirely agree with the suggestions that have come from all sides of the house that money spent in research is money well spent, and I include in that money spent in improving the design of housing accommodation. Much has been accomplished already in that regard by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Prior to the National Housing Act, home building standards in Canada were nothing like what they are today. The advent of the National Housing Act brought about a distinct improvement in the construction standards of our homes. The same thing has happened in regard to the planning of homes. While perhaps it is true that not more than one-quarter of the homes being built today come directly under the National Housing Act, it is equally true that many private home builders are using the well designed plans which anyone can get from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at nominal cost.
In addition to the saving that can be effected by reducing the annual payments required to service land, I think a distinct saving can be effected in the actual purchase of land. In many of these fringe land developments I believe land can be provided at a cost which would permit lots to be sold for not more than $200 or $300 each, instead of the present going rate, which I believe is $500 or $600.
So I urge the minister to do everything he can to get low-rental housing for the needy workmen of this country, and at the same time go as far as he can to make all those advantages also available to people who want to own their own homes. And before I reach the concluding portion of my address let me urge once more that private members can make a real contribution to the solution of this problem. I live in the district between Hamilton and Toronto; my riding fronts on lake Ontario. That district has participated perhaps as largely as any district in Canada in the tremendous development going on today. The builders in my riding are on their toes. I have tried in every way to help them and today in Halton we have our building problem well under control. Under the integrated housing program something over 11,000 homes have been built for veterans.
I should like to comment for a moment on that feature of the National Housing Act.
National Housing Act
Under that scheme the builder is restricted on the resale price to an extremely modest profit. Under that scheme he must give priority in the sale of those homes to veterans, but in return for that the builder is given priority for all building materials. The government also gives the builder an undertaking that any unsold houses will be taken off his hands. In two short years, as a result of that, approximately 11,000 housing units were produced.
Then there was the unfortunate experience with the Bow River construction out west. This scheme involved approximately 40-houses. As a result of the failure of that scheme, what do we find? The member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) urged that certain safeguards and restrictions should be imposed to protect the purchaser. Those restrictions were imposed and they are rather onerous. What has been the result of that? The number of houses built under the integrated plan this year is approximately 2,300. The member for Bow River got his restrictions, and we got the results. I wish to urge the minister to revise those restrictions. I do not believe the whole integrated plan should fall into disuse simply because of one incident that happened in Bow River. I should like to urge also, as a control against builders taking: unreasonable profits, that it might be wise to introduce a ceiling price on houses built under the National Housing Act. Perhaps this should not be a rigid ceiling price in that it should allow a little more profit than is allowed under the integrated plan, but I. think that is a good way of guarding against excessive prices.
I shall turn now to another plan of the; Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I refer to the rental insurance plan which came into force a year ago last July. Under this plan loans up to 85 per cent of the cost of the project are available to owners. The, interest rate is four and one-quarter per cent. The rental insurance premium costs, in round figures, another quarter per cent of the face of the mortgage, for which the owner is insured up to 85 per cent of the agreed rentals. The insurance is for a period of twenty or thirty years, whichever period the owner chooses. This is a safe investment and it is a profitable investment for a builder who is interested in that type of building. The only string on that is that if depressed times return and the owner has to draw on the rental insurance to a greater amount than the total of one year's rental, then the government reserves the right to buy back the building at the agreed price less the yearly principal payments that have been paid off the mortgage. Under this rental insurance plan, two and a half per cent of the principal is retired

National Housing Act
annually and, of course, the rental guarantee drops correspondingly each year. I would say that the premium which is being paid would go a long way towards meeting any liability which will occur under this insurance scheme. In other words, there is very little of the subsidy feature in this scheme.
Under this scheme in slightly more than a year, 7,900 rental accommodation units have been built. On checking the records, I find that Quebec leads all other provinces in Canada by a substantial amount. In Quebec approximately 5,400 of these rental insurance units were built in slightly over a year. Ontario lags behind in this field. Whereas the province of Quebec built approximately 5,400 units, there were less than 1,900 units built in the whole of the province of Ontario. Once again, I should like to ask my hon. friend the member for Eglinton to get busy in the city of Toronto. Practically none of these units have been built in that city. The hon. member would be doing a good turn to the people in Toronto who want decent rental accommodation. He would be doing a good turn to the builder whom he interests in this scheme, and I think he would be doing himself a good turn because, after he has done some work of that sort, I do not think he will feel so frustrated as he obviously does today.
I turn now to co-operative housing. This is one field in which the members of the house could get busy. I trust the house will pardon another personal reference, but I helped to organize eleven of these schemes in the last two years involving something over 400 housing units. Two such schemes are in progress in Oakville at the moment. I shall tell you about one of them. A group of about fifteen chaps, most of them veterans, came to see me five or six months ago and talked over the project. I helped them get it started. These veterans are building fine modern homes with three bedrooms, all fully equipped and modern in every respect, at a cost of approximately $6,700 each. The men are turning in $300 worth of work on each of the homes and are doing some general over-all work as well. The carrying charges including the mortgage, taxes, fire insurance, water rates and so on will add up to just under $45 per month. That is the way I like to see Canadian boys behave. I would far rather see that type of construction, that type of home occupancy, where a man has a real stake in the welfare of the country.
I should like to say just a word about the over-all operation of the National Housing Act. In the past some members have commented on the small amount of housing in Canada built under Central Mortgage and Housing. I believe these remarks are largely

the result of misunderstanding and misinformation. I should like to put a few of the general figures on the record. Since its inception and up to July 31, 1949, 67,000 N.H.A. housing units have been built in this country. The total of the outstanding loans as of the same date is approximately $340 million. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that is a stupendous contribution. In addition to that, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation manages something over 40,000 government-owned homes.
There is one feature which I think has not been recognized. It is that the Central Mortgage and Housing funds or N.H.A. funds are largely responsible for practically all the speculative building undertaken in Canada. Funds for that type of building in sufficient amounts were not available from private institutions. We would not have had these speculatively built houses if it were not for N.H.A. funds and, as a result, we would not have had the large quantity of houses which we have. In looking over the whole picture, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we have every right to be proud, and that the private members should go to work.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benidickson for the second reading of Bill No. 119, to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, at the last sitting when this bill was discussed I pointed out the steps necessary to be taken by any company which desires to build a pipe line in Canada. I said that the first requirement under the Pipe Lines Act is that the company shall be incorporated by act of this parliament. I pointed out that the company must
180S	HOUSE OF
Prairie Transmission Lines next acquire the gas sufficient to justify a pipe line, by contract with producing companies or by other means. I then pointed out that the company must obtain an export licence from the province of Alberta which, through its own legislation, has retained jurisdiction over the export of gas from that province. I then pointed out that the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada must be satisfied with the route of the pipe line and satisfied with all particulars regarding the construction of the pipe line.
I stated that one requirement of the board of transport commissioners would be the assurance that an export licence under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act would be forthcoming. That act is administered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and its function is to make sure that electricity or fluids are not exported until the present and future requirements of Canada are satisfied. It is therefore seen that there are ample safeguards for the public interest of Canada.
A good deal has been said about possible routes of the pipe line. A good many uninformed assertions have been made in the house in that regard. I know nothing about the pipe line company which is asking for incorporation under this bill; but I do know something about the interests that are asking for incorporation under another bill now before the house. I know that that company has surveyed five routes from Alberta to the Pacific coast, and that one of them at least is an all-Canadian route. There is no difference whatever between my opinion and opinions expressed here that Vancouver must not be on the end of the pipe line. Vancouver must be served before any considerable service is taken off for supply to the United States. Under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act that requirement would have to be complied with before any export permit will be given by the department of which I am the minister.
However, I do think that these acts should be studied, and studied very carefully. I should like to know much more about the incorporation asked for in the bill about which I am speaking than I know at the present time. But the place to obtain that information is in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to which this bill will be referred, and before which the sponsors of the bill will appear to make their case for incorporation.
I will say this, however, that since incorporation by act of parliament is a requirement of the Pipe Lines Act, that incorporation should not be refused on trivial grounds. It seems obvious to me that if a responsible group of men, be they Canadians or Americans, properly financed and having

the proper background of experience, apply to this parliament for incorporation, they are entitled to incorporate.
I should like also to say a word about what seems obviously to be a filibuster in connection with these bills. The government will not permit any small number of members to prevent this house as a whole from voting on a private bill. If these bills continue to be talked out in the limited time permitted for private bills, the government will ask the house to suspend the rules and provide whatever time is required to finish the discussion and to obtain a vote on such bills.
I might say the house has granted one franchise for a pipe line for gas in a western direction and a pipe line for gas in an eastern direction. As the situation stands today, the incorporators of each of those two bills have a monopoly, so far as gas moving in either direction is concerned. My hon. friends of the C.C.F. party have a good deal to say about monopolies, and yet we find them very busy filibustering so that the monopoly on the pipe line situation can be maintained.
The province of Alberta will, in the end, decide with which incorporated company it wishes to do business. That province has expressed the desire that it shall have the choice as between several companies, and there are obvious advantages in that procedure as far as Alberta is concerned. Therefore, I hope that these pipe line bills will be examined and if they are properly sponsored I hope that this house will grant the incorporations.

I have nothing further to say on this bill and I would not have said what I have said tonight if the minister had not spoken as he did. But now that the question has been brought out in the open we shall see who is behind these bills.

Mr. Speaker, as the one member of this party who spoke on the previous bill, not on this one, I want to make it quite clear that what I said on that occasion expressed exactly what I felt, that these pipe 45781-115
Prairie Transmission Lines lines going through the United States are not going to serve the best interests of the province from which I come. I felt that there should be included in that bill a clause containing a promise that the pipe lines would go through the dominion to Vancouver. I gave my reasons for objecting and I think they are sincere. I resent the minister's suggestion that we are filibustering when we put these claims before the house. Now that the minister has full knowledge of the conditions under which I spoke, now that he knows that I was the only speaker, I think he should retract the suggestion he made.

Mr. Speaker, as one of the two members from southern British Columbia whose constituents are greatly concerned with this bill I should like to express the opinion of those constituents. I was surprised to hear the minister suggest that this group was conducting a filibuster. Originally it was intended that only the two members primarily concerned, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) and myself, would speak on this or the related bill. I was fully aware that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) did not intend to speak. I am sure if the records of this house are read it will be proved that the hon. member for Yale and I rise to speak only when we feel we have occasion to say something and it is our duty to do so.
I am going to deal for a few minutes with this bill to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited and express the opinions of the people whom I represent. It is strange that this bill and the related bill to incorporate the Alberta Natural Gas Company are sponsored by Manitoba members. Apparently there was no British Columbia member who was ready to stand up and sponsor either of these bills.
Manitoba and Ontario members.

Pardon me, Manitoba and Ontario members. I think that is rather significant. In speaking at this time I feel I am doing my duty in expressing the opinions of the great majority of the people whom I have the honour to represent. I am quite certain that if a plebiscite were taken on these bills 95 per cent of the people of Alberta and British Columbia would vote in support of the action taken by those opposing the bills in this house.
There has been an indication of united action by members of the Conservative, the C.C.F., the Social Credit and the Liberal parties. Hon. members of those parties have considered it their duty to express their opinions with regard to the protection of

Prairie Transmission Lines Canadian natural resources and Canadian interests. We have a perfect right to do that as representatives of the people.
Strangely enough, just yesterday I was talking to a person who had recently come to Ottawa from Washington state. These pipe line bills are of considerable interest to the people of Idaho and Washington because the introduction of gas and oil from Canada will mean a great deal to the development of industry in those states. I am speaking only from information given to me, but I think what I have been told indicates that we should be careful in giving these wide powers to these companies.
The newspapers in Idaho and Washington have published maps which show the wide distribution that is to be made of these natural resources to the cities, towns and small communities in those states. Not one of those maps I am informed shows the pipe line returning to Canada to serve Vancouver and our coastal cities. This bill is most important to the people of the interior of British Columbia as it provides for the transportation and exportation of natural resources in the form of oil and gas. In addition you will find on examining the bill that it confers very wide powers on the company concerned, the holding of lands, the building of pipe lines, the operation of air services, and telephone and other communications. In fact the privileges granted to this company, if the bill is adopted by the house, are so wide that they are causing some of the members from British Columbia serious concern.
Before proceeding to deal briefly with my argument-and I am not speaking for the sake of holding up the bill-I must say that I think we made a mistake when we passed the general pipe lines bill last session, and the other bills associated with it. They were introduced during the latter part of the session and did not receive sufficient attention. I am quite sure that many of the members who supported the pipe lines bill did not visualize for a moment the export of gas into United States territory before serving Canadian requirements fully. I am quite sure that aspect of the situation was not given consideration when that measure was passed.
I think the time has come for us to give earnest and careful consideration, as the minister mentioned, to these pipe line bills. What we do at this time may mean much in the future to the advantage or disadvantage of Canada. At this time I wish to emphasize the point of view of members of the C.C.F. group with respect to a measure of this type. We favour the operation of pipe lines as a public utility. We believe they should be owned by a crown company, and operated by


the crown in order to ensure the fair distribution of gas for industrial and community development and domestic use. This is a new development which will be considerable in the future, and I think the profits will be large in the days to come. We should therefore ensure that the profits made in the distribution and transportation of these products will be returned to the public exchequer.
We are often told that the capital cannot be found in Canada to develop such huge undertakings. I understand these projects will cost from $100 million to $125 million. In my opinion that is not a large sum of money for the Dominion of Canada to invest if the pipe lines were organized under a crown company. I think we would be protecting Canadian consumers. We would have complete control over the transportation and fair distribution of the commodity, and the state would reap the profits. That is not the policy of the government. Their policy is free enterprise. They do not believe in the public ownership of pipe lines through crown companies. Therefore, not finding it possible to have our ideas given effect to by this parliament, we feel it is our duty to do the best we can to protect Canadian interests under the existing situation.
First we are opposing the bill

and I am speaking particularly of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) and myself-because we believe the route to be followed should be stated therein. If the sponsor of the measure wishes to see it passed readily by the house, all he has to do is to rise in his place and assure members of the house that an allCanadian route will be followed before the entry of the pipe line into the United States. I realize that under the Pipe Lines Act parliament has given authority to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to decide such questions, but it is my contention that in such an important matter, and in view of public opinion as expressed by the people at the head of the lakes, parliament should at least decide the approximate route that the pipe lines should follow. I believe we should follow the procedure adopted in granting charters to railways when we grant incorporation to companies which are going to transport gas or oil. The routes which it is intended the pipe lines should follow should be designated and approved by the house.
Second, I believe Canadian needs should be met first before any export of oil or gas from Canadian soil is permitted. There is no guarantee to that effect in the bill. Third, I believe the house should be fully informed as to the persons who are financing this company. We see mentioned in the bill various solicitors and persons of the city of

Toronto and other places, but that does not give to the house real information as to the individuals who are financing the company. I am opposing the bill at the present time, and I am supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) until I am assured that an allCanadian route via the Kettle valley, Hope, and then down the Fraser valley to Vancouver will be followed so that the coastal cities and the interior of British Columbia will be assured of service first.
If the proposed United States route is adopted it will mean that the pipe line will, from our present information, traverse only a short distance in the eastern portion of British Columbia before entering the United States at Kingsgate and give first service to United States industries and communities. Large sections of the southern interior of British Columbia would, if that were the case, be denied the advantages of this gas and oil. As I said before, in my opinion Canada's natural resources should be used to develop Canadian industries and Canadian communities first. There is great need for the development of secondary industry in the interior of British Columbia. In fact it is the primary need to bring our economy into a proper balance. I am sure the minister will agree with me on that. The boards of trade of Trail, Nelson, Penticton, Kelowna and all the smaller interior communities, the farmers' organizations and co-operatives, in fact all public-spirited bodies, are most anxious to see the development of secondary industry in the interior of British Columbia.
For that reason members from British Columbia intend to do all they can to assure the availability of these natural resources to the interior towns and communities for the development of the necessary secondary industries in the Kootenay, Okanagan and Fraser valleys. Then again, if the pipe line is routed through the United States it will mean that the greater part of it will be under foreign control. There is no question about it. Once it enters the United States they can determine the destination of the line. A branch line from the United States to Vancouver and other Canadian coastal points will mean the possibility that they may not receive all the gas they eventually will require for industrial expansion and domestic use. I think that is a very undesirable feature of any proposal that these pipe lines should first enter the United States and then return to Canada. I think it also stands to reason that, as Vancouver and the other coastal cities will be at the end of the pipe line, the cost will be higher to them on that account.
