Prairie Transmission Lines
Before concluding I wish to deal briefly with what I consider are the advantages to Canadians and to the people of British Columbia of an all-Canadian route. If the pipe line follows the valleys of the Kettle and the Fraser to the coast, the gas or oil exported therefrom will include charges for transportation. Therefore I am of the opinion that a very much larger amount of United States funds would be payable in Canada than if the gas and oil were exported to the United States at some point before the line went far into British Columbia. Again, the construction of nearly 900 miles of pipe line in my province, if an all-Canadian route were followed, would mean the employment of a large number of Canadians; and I believe we in this house should consider that point. It would also mean immense markets for Canadian materials, for Canadian steel, pipe, valves, fittings, compressors, cement and lumber; and a large market, while the line was being built, for Canadian farm commodities. I believe those facts have to be considered seriously. All those expenditures would be lost to Canada if this line did not follow an all-Canadian route. Later on the maintenance of 900 miles of pipe line would mean a continuous and large expenditure which would provide permanent employment for many Canadians and an assured market for large quantities of materials. The construction of nearly 900 miles of pipe line on Canadian soil would return large revenues to the province of British Columbia in the form of sales tax during construction and by way of other taxes after the line was completed. Speaking as a British Columbia member I believe we certainly must give consideration to that fact.
In view of my firm belief that Canadian natural resources should be used first to develop Canadian communities and Canadian industries; in view of the fact that we must first consider employment for Canadians, markets for Canadian products and revenue for the Canadian exchequer, all of which will flow from the development of Canadian natural resources within Canada, it is my intention to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church).

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have had anything at all to say on these bills incorporating companies to construct pipe lines. I must say I support the view just expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). That is quite a concession, because I seldom support a socialist in anything he proposes. However, the hon. gentleman and I are good

Prairie Transmission Lines friends, and since he has thrown in the sponge with respect to pipe lines being socialized, I can support him now.
I support what he has said with respect to an all-Canadian route. I do so not because I particularly want to speak on the matter but because on the train on my way to Ottawa I had quite an extended conversation with an Alberta oil executive, who expressed the view that the pipe line should go through the Kettle valley, following an all-Canadian route. His position was that there was no reason why the larger cities in the northwestern United States should not be supplied by the same pipe line. He went on to explain, though it really does not require much explanation, that if the pipe line ran through the Crowsnest pass, Kettle valley and the Fraser valley, it would provide oil and gas to many small communities along the way. Some of them are not so small; some are growing rapidly. There is the city of Nelson, which is a growing community. I was there this summer; I am not quite sure what the population is, but it is quite a nice little community. It is not far from Nelson to Spokane, which is a large city in the state of Washington, and it would not be difficult to construct a feeder line from the all-Canadian pipe line to Spokane, the largest city until you get to Seattle. Then it would not be so very far from the pipe line running through the Fraser valley down to Seattle. So it would be quite reasonable to have the pipe line follow an all-Canadian route to supply our own communities with oil and gas, and at the same time construct feeder lines to these larger cities to the south.
I certainly support the very reasonable request that has been made by the hon. member for Kootenay West, that the sponsor of this bill should say now what route it is intended to have this pipe line follow. Of *course that does not mean very much, either, even if we have the assurance of the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill. Unless there is something in the bill itself, any assurance that may be given is not worth a great deal. I do not mean to cast any reflection upon anyone who may give an assurance, but business is business; and after the assurance is given, if it is considered wise to have the pipe line follow some other route, that will be done.
Before I resume my seat I want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that I do not think he scares anyone when he accuses any group or any individuals of creating a filibuster. I am rather charmed with the word, and I do not mind a bit being party to a filibuster. I have been in this house long enough to know that, even on a measure of this kind, if a minister of the crown can gather enough support through the


party machinery there is not a ghost of a chance of that measure being defeated unless we want to exercise the only prerogative left to us in that case, and talk it out. To some that may appear not altogether ethical; but if we are so convinced that the thing is wrong and we do not want it to be done, no minister of the crown is going to scare any of the members by saying they are creating a filibuster.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I have had a little publicity out of this. I have been accused of organizing a filibuster, according to some newspapers. I did not know I had sufficient influence to control such independent members as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and a few others. I am rather flattered to be accused of organizing a so-called filibuster. That seems rather peculiar to me when I recall that the sponsor of one of these very bills spoke for forty-one minutes to talk out a certain bill. You can check that in Hansard; I remember because I have now become one of the old-timers in this house. I did not know until tonight that the government was interested in this bill. I am going to tell you the reason why I am interested in it. Last year I sponsored a bill on behalf of the Westcoast Transmission Company whose directors are the wealthiest and most responsible and reliable men in the province of British Columbia. These men did not try to influence me in my stand on the matter. Two of the directors of that company were in Ottawa last week, and neither of them saw me.
The people of the province of British Columbia are interested in the matter, at least some of us, and I am glad some of the C.C.F. members have spoken on the subject, first as Canadians and secondly as inhabitants of British Columbia. We have no desire to start dissension between the east and west. We want no favours or concessions from the east, nor do we want, and particularly through you, any concessions to certain members from the east at our expense. We are trying to build up British Columbia. Apparently some members have never heard of that attempt. Within the last week, natural gas wells have been brought into existence. Some members have apparently never heard of that, but they should keep abreast of what is happening in Canada. Never mind the United States. I was born in the United States; I have every pride in that country; but I am a Canadian first, last and always.
I was glad to hear the minister say tonight, and I want to be corrected in this if I am wrong in my understanding, that no matter

what company has the charter gas will not be exported until after it goes to Vancouver. Am I correct in that?
That is correct. I said Canada's present and future needs would be provided for before any export is permitted.
I am glad to hear the minister say that. From that it is obvious that, no matter which company gets the charter, the route will be an all-Canadian route.
Oh, no.

Some of my friends who are not experienced in the law should study it. Once gas or oil is exported to the United States, it becomes an international matter. Neither Canada nor British Columbia has any say whether the surplus will be allowed back into Canada from Seattle. Hon. members can check on that point if they wish. The power situation in Ontario is a case in point, as I believe the leader of the opposition knows. Once these products get over to the United States they become matters of international concern, and Canada cannot say whether the surplus will be returned. The question has to be decided on an international basis.
The United States is a growing country. How do we know there will be any brought back? I should like to repeat what the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said; if you took a vote in the province of British Columbia today you could not get 18 people to vote for the route through the United States. Here are two companies, and I have no doubt one is a good company and the other is backed by pure promoters. I have no doubt one company is bona fide. There are 18 members from the province of British Columbia now, and for the first time British Columbia has the proper representation. There are at least 12 Liberals out of the 18 members. Neither of these companies could get a sponsor for these bills from amongst the 18 members. One had to be sponsored by a member from Ontario and the other by a member from Manitoba. Is it not quite obvious from that what the people of British Columbia think of those companies?
In my riding, I do not have to curry favour or make threats. The people of my riding will tell George Cruickshank what they think of him when the next election comes. I am not worried half as much as some people here should be about the results in their ridings. I know what the people of British Columbia think.
I should like to point out a few facts in connection with this matter. I pointed out that the Westcoast Transmission Company
Prairie Transmission Lines has invested hundreds of thousands of dollars of their own money, not any promotional money, in exploring routes and developing the natural resources of Canada. That company has deposited with the government of Alberta approximately $600,000. To some people in the east $600,000 means nothing, but to the people from the land of the Stampeders $600,000 is a lot of money. I sponsored this company simply because it proposes to build an all-Canadian route. The company has $3 million in reserve to develop and exploit the oil and gas resources of the Dominion of Canada. They are not fly-by-night promoter? by any manner or means. The company has the money available to build these lines.
It has been estimated that it will probably cost $170 million to build the pipe line no matter which company builds it. The money will be raised in Canada and the United States. It will be raised by any one of the incorporated companies in exactly the same way. Someone has said something about forty minutes, and I hope it was not a member from British Columbia. I will take my stand right now and vote on the matter as a British Columbia member. Just to show who these people are who are in the Westcoast Transmission Company, may I give you the names of some of the companies in the group. There is the Pacific Petroleums Limited, Calgary, which is a subsidiary. The Peace River Natural Gas Company Limited; Sunray Oil Corporation of Tulsa and Los Angeles-1 wish some of my friends would check on these companies. There is the Pacific Western Oil Corporation of Los Angeles and the Tide Water Associated Oil Company of San Francisco. All of these companies have several hundred million dollars behind them. They are the companies through which the Westcoast Transmission Company will finance the undertaking.
Then, there is Eastman, Dillon and Company of New York. Even some of the junior members from Ontario should know whom that company represents. Some of them may have heard of the Morgans of New York. I am not trying to talk this bill out, but I could easily do so if I wished, since there is only ten minutes left. I do want to put on the record what the attorney general of the province of British Columbia said about these pipe lines when he appeared before the board of transport commissioners. Surely the attorney general of British Columbia should have some standing. He said:
Mr. Chief Commissioner and Mr. Assistant Chief Commissioner and commissioners of the board: The government of British Columbia is very, very strongly supporting the proposal to export gas from northern Alberta through British Columbia to Vancouver.

Prairie Transmission Lines
We feel that it would be a great step forward in the development of northern British Columbia,-
I am surprised now that we have not heard something from northern British Columbia.
-and we are in duty bound of course to make the representations because we enjoy a franchise from the people of British Columbia in the last election to start a survey for gas.
Now, I had hoped before making any special submission that I would have had an opportunity of listening to the evidence that will be presented on behalf of this applicant as to their financial possibilities and as to their plans and so on. All I can say now is that we generally support the proposal to export gas in this manner.
If I may make a few observations as to the points I consider should be mentioned,-
Do not forget this is the attorney general of the province of British Columbia speaking. His government was just returned with the strongest mandate that any government has had for many years. This is the attorney general's submission to the board of transport commissioners.
-if you first have a permit to operate, I am afraid if that decision is taken it will be a very, very long time before we will ever carry out the proposal which our government had in mind, that is to export through this particular territory. That had :he advantage of not only opening up the northern part of British Columbia, it comes down through some sixteen I think very important constituencies in that province, but it also had the advantage that it would lead to the development of our own oil reserves in the north,-
I want to repeat that: "our own oil reserves in the north". We have every reason to believe, and I am quoting the premier of my own province, that we have in northern British Columbia oil resources equal to those in Alberta; we have every reason to believe that in our own northern British Columbia we have coal resources unequalled anywhere else in Canada. Should we not develop those resources? To continue the quotation:
-because we feel we have a great potential oil and gas field in northern British Columbia as they have in Alberta. We have very sound reasons for that. We had the report of geologists and our own investigation. We felt that if this pipe line was built in the manner that is suggested that we could look for the development of gas lands in northern British Columbia, the gas to be picked up on the way. So that this is very-
The Chief Commissioner: Is there some development there now?

There is some development
going on, some slight development going on. But we feel that would be accelerated.
I want to point out to the board this, that you have an entirely different situation in northern British Columbia and northern Alberta than you have in southern Alberta. There you have towns, you have a market for your gas, and that undoubtedly has been a factor which influenced companies in spending their money for the production of gas. But in the north if you must wait to find the amount of gas which will comply with the requirements of the Alberta government I am afraid we will wait a very long time, because what company or what individual is going to spend money exploring to find out if the gas is there unless there is a market? I mean we have the same situation in
[Mr. Cruickshank.}
regard to oil. The first thing any company would ask, or any investor, would be to say "What are we going to do with it after we find it?"
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word to the house about all these various little settlements that are mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), before I go on with what the attorney general had to say. We have heard it said, and we presume that it was meant seriously, that it was the desire of our great leaders to decentralize industry and to build up the smaller communities where the labour situation is easier and the living costs are less. As I understand it, we have today a committee of this house visiting a certain plant. If war should come it is a most essential thing to Canada that we should have our industry decentralized. How can we do it if we are to place in the hands of what has been called a monopoly greater difficulties in bringing this about?
The best speech made on this subject certainly was not made by any member of the government. It was made last year by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) who said-and I am speaking from memory now-that he was surprised that the directors of the Canadian National Railways had not taken more interest in this matter, and that they should have developed this resource, not any private company. But it was obvious to everyone that you cannot have some five or six companies operating. It would not be possible to finance them; and to finance the operation, it could not be possible for them to construct five or six lines across Canada.
Just to surprise some of my junior friends, let me say that I am not going to talk until nine o'clock.
Hear, hear.
There are other members who can go on talking until then. I am speaking on the amendment. I have plenty of chances to speak on the two main bills.
Carried.
Go on and finish.

I am getting a little bit of assistance from some of my friends who apparently have never seen the west, let alone taken any interest in it. I am disappointed that there are not more of my friends from the province of British Columbia here tonight. If there were, I would be delighted to have a vote on this matter right now. It is exactly nine o'clock now, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
No.
It is not nine o'clock.
There is one minute more.
Question.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Carried.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
It being nine o'clock, the house will resume the business which was interrupted at six o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) on a most constructive speech. In my opinion, housing is the greatest national problem we have in Canada today. We have other national problems such as social security, full employment and national health but in one way or another they are all related to the housing problem. A man might have a steady job, adequate insurance and pension for old age, but if he has not a decent place in which to live and raise his family, he has not social security.
Inadequate and overcrowded housing is the breeding ground of physical disease, mental disease and social disease in that it has a bearing on juvenile delinquency and crime. A housing program of sufficient volume to meet the needs of the Canadian people is and always will be a stabilizing influence in the over-all economy of the nation. While the wages paid in the construction industry are not large, they are largely spent for the necessities of life and almost immediately find their way into local trade channels. The present housing crisis is partly the aftermath of the war, but it had its beginning, in my opinion, as far back as twenty-five years ago. Following the first great war the radio and the automobile were developed, accompanied by instalment buying, or pay-as-you-go financing.
We needed more and better housing in the 1920's, but this was not considered to be a social problem; it was one for the individuals concerned. We had not yet learned to blame our troubles on the government. The automobile and the radio captured the imagination of the buying public, and the result was that a large percentage of the purchasing of that generation was diverted to channels other than housing. The buying public always call the tune and get what they want. The result was that there was little technical improvement or advance in housing methods or in the
National Housing Act
planning of housing during the 1920's. With the economic breakdown and depression, the housing industry practically went out of existence. The government of the day told us to tighten our belts and to go back to the farm. A large-scale housing program at that time not only would have provided a great deal of employment but would have created a great national asset in the form of housing, from the lack of which we are still suffering today. The government of the day preferred to pay direct relief which had no lasting result but to increase the national debt.
I do not think that progress in housing stopped entirely during the 1930's. It was during that period that insulation, improved plumbing, improved electrical equipment and many other technical advances were developed. But in so far as the general public was concerned, it meant little because they could not afford to buy. The automobile, which is always an expensive luxury, and a fast depreciating asset, became the Bennett buggy. With the change of government in Ottawa there was a change for the better, and with the passing of the Dominion Housing Act, and later the National Housing Act and the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, the industry began to improve, especially in the provinces where local governments were willing to co-operate.
In my own province of Alberta the National Housing Act did not become fully operative until 1944. At the beginning of the war the building industry was mobilized for the war effort. Supply industries and all available manpower were conscripted to build ships, barracks, factories and houses for war workers. For obvious reasons there was very little civilian housing built during the war.
At the end of the war the government felt obliged to provide shelter for returning veterans, a large number of whom had married. Large sums were spent and in some localities every available building was converted to temporary shelter. The operations of Wartime Housing Limited, which was incorporated in the first place to provide housing for war workers, were extended into peacetime. This same agency has operated to provide emergency shelter for veterans in areas where the need was most acute; and I believe it has done much to relieve the pressure which might otherwise have become explosive.
At the end of the war the building industry and the lumber industry were still geared for war production. Like other industries they took some time to reconvert to peacetime needs. That time lag, together with the unprecedented demand for materials, has caused serious shortages which have plagued

National Housing Act
the industry ever since the war. It is only in recent months that the supply of materials has anywhere nearly met the demand.
In spite of the shortage of materials the house building industry has made a remarkable recovery. We in Canada have built more houses, on a per capita basis, than any other nation in the world for which we have statistics, including Great Britain and the United States. Our standard of housing has greatly improved. The houses of today are planned for convenience and use rather than for appearance. A modern house is insulated, kitchens are modern, electrical installations are elaborate, and plumbing has been greatly improved.
The saving in interest rates alone, the 41 per cent under a National Housing Act loan today, as compared with 7 per cent which was common before the war, accounts for a saving of approximately $10 a month on the purchase of a $6,000 house over a twenty-five-year period.
Our national income is at an all-time high. It has more than doubled. Employment is more universal than ever before. Today's construction costs are high; but considering the improvements in housing, the saving in interest rates and the high level of employment and income, I believe the average Canadian is better able to pay for housing at today's costs than ever before.
The housing industry in my opinion is just as efficient as any other industry or profession. The costs have not risen any more, comparatively, than they have for food, or any other costs of living. We are suffering from the war, and the depression which preceded the war. During the depression few if any young men entered the building trades for the simple reason that there was no work for them. Also the trades did not pay enough to warrant young men making it their life work. Even today a lot of people think that building workers are overpaid, but I contend they are not. Owing to the seasonal nature of the work the average building worker does not make much more than $200 a month. If that is too high a salary, then they are overpaid. The average weekly wage rate in the construction industry as at the end of July, 1949, was $43.23 per week.
Soon after the war many young men entered the building trades, and as they acquire skill the over-all efficiency of the industry is improving. The availability of labour-saving power tools and the introduction of new materials and techniques will from now on be a factor in increased production as well as in the reduction of costs.
Many who criticize today's increased costs are prone to forget the great improvement that has taken place in housing. Also they

forget that pre-war housing was produced at very low wages, and if we are to revert to 1930 prices we will also have 1930 wages, with the accompanying unemployment and breadlines.
Home ownership has a stabilizing influence in the family life which is reflected in the community and in the national life. In my opinion it is the best hedge we have against communism. This is evidenced by the fact that in countries where communistic governments gain control the first thing they do is to liquidate property holders. Food, clothing and shelter are the three necessities of life which we cannot escape. We must pay for them. Food and clothing are completely expendable, but not necessarily shelter.
We pay for our landlord's house, or we pay for our own. If we live in a subsidized house we pay for it partly by taxes. Home ownership has the added advantage that every monthly payment adds to one's estate. By wise purchase rather than renting the cost of shelter becomes a profitable investment. All the purchase of a house actually costs is the down payment. Monthly payments for principal, interest and taxes under the National Housing Act are in most cases less than rent for similar accommodation. Added advantages are the building of an estate, security of tenure, and the other satisfactions including pride of ownership.
There are those who advocate subsidized housing and government-owned rentals. Subsidized housing is a negative approach to the problem. It is in effect subsidizing low wages. I believe Canada can provide an income for all able-bodied persons who are willing to work, an income sufficient to provide the necessities of life, to raise and educate a family and to provide shelter for that family.
Subsidies must come from taxes. Taxes come from the working population, directly and indirectly. If the majority in the country are in need of subsidy, as hon. members of the C.C.F. would have us believe, then it is only a matter of time until we would all be pulled down to the same level. I do not believe that the young people of this country want subsidies; all they want is a chance to help themselves.
In my opinion it should be made possible for young people to begin the purchase of their homes when they first form their families. In my experience as a builder for years I have found that the average person buying a house was in middle age. The reason for that was that it took him that long to save the money necessary to finance the down payment. Children of these people were usually in high school. The result was that they had the maximum use of their new homes for only six to ten years, until the

children left home. The children went out to support their own families and had to go through the same process of living in undesirable quarters. The net result then, and the same applies to some extent today, was that the average citizen spent his early childhood and married life under unsatisfactory housing conditions.
There are those who say that the financial risk of a home-ownership scheme is too great, but I say it is very small. The loans will be secured, first by the building, and second by the credit of the young people of this country. If those two securities are not good, then there is nothing of value in this country. The urge for home ownership is fundamental. It is natural and instinctive to all creation. Even in England under a socialist government, where only one house in five is produced by private enterprise for private ownership, the desire for home ownership is once more becoming very evident. I should like to quote from the Overseas Daily Mail, a London newspaper, of October 8, 1949, as follows:
Britons prefer to own their own homes.
The building societies year book for 1949 just published shows that during 1948 building society membership increased by 53,000 and now more than totals 4,196,000. Borrowers increased by 23,000 and investors by 42,386. The sum advanced to borrowers during the year, largely for buying homes, was 264,000 pounds, the highest on record.
Commenting on this the book says. The facts lead to the inescapable conclusion that in spite of the lavish sums lavished on public authority housing, the average citizen of this country prefers to own his house and is willing to pay for it if he is given a chance.
Building societies have been most successful for the last 100 years in England enabling hundreds of private citizens to purchase their homes built by private contractors and through private enterprise.
I would say to those who defend the system of government-owned rental housing that that also has many evils. In the final analysis it is the same system as that used in Russia and other communistically inclined countries. I think it should be used here only in cases of emergency. To my hon. friends of the C.C.F. and others who advocate subsidized housing I should like to tell an old story. A certain farmer was very thrifty. In the fall of the year he and his family gathered vegetables and fruit and brought them into the basement for use by the family during the winter months. Being thrifty they gathered up all the cull and windfall apples and the family were instructed to use those first. They did this and the cull apples lasted during the fall. Then when they opened the barrels of good apples they found that the top layers showed signs of decay. Being thrifty the farmer instructed them to use the decayed apples because they could not afford to waste them. Being
National Housing Act
obedient the family did so, but by the time they reached the next lot of apples they found more signs of decay. The final result was that while the family had apples all winter, they used only decayed apples.
Subsidies work in the same way. If you subsidize the lower strata at the expense of the other taxpayers, it is only a matter of time until they will all need subsidies, and then what do we do? I recognize of course that there are those who because of extreme misfortune, physical disability or old age are unable to help themselves and therefore must receive assistance from the state. But as a general policy, and considering the fact that the production of houses is limited by the capacity of the industry to produce, I believe we should concentrate first on the great middle band who are able and anxious to help themselves. If and when we satisfy the needs of this great middle group it will be time enough to consider subsidies and slum clearance, except in cases of extreme emergency. I believe there are still some emergency areas in Canada where government action will probably have to be taken.
By concentrating first on the middle band, a large number in the lower income strata can be lifted and assisted to help themselves. If we concentrate first on those in the lower income band and assist them by means of subsidies, which must be paid by the taxpaying public, there is every danger that a large percentage of those in the middle band will be discouraged and forced into the lower group and will themselves become eligible for subsidies.
I believe we have only two alternatives. First, there is the positive approach to the problem which places the emphasis on home ownership, even with small down payments, and which will enable people to help themselves, with the government assuming the risk of having to subsidize such a scheme only if and when we run into a major depression and purchasers are forced into default. The other alternative, which is the negative approach, is to provide subsidies now rather than take a chance on the future.
Let us review the situation as it exists today. Employment and income are at an all-time high, but wartime savings and gratuities are largely spent. Because of the high level of prosperity we have an unprecedented demand for separate housing accommodation. People are no longer contented to live in shared quarters. Because of the high level of prosperity the marriage rate is at an all-time high and the new family formations alone almost equal our present production of houses. There is a decided trend and desire

National Housing Act
on the part of young people to marry young and raise a family. The first thought now seems to be a home rather than an automobile.
The mechanization of farms and the prosperity of the agricultural industry have caused a large exodus from the farms to urban centres. We have a large backlog of need as a legacy from the war and pre-war years. We are becoming socially conscious and greater attention is now being paid to public health. Because housing is a social as well as a physical problem, all levels of government have a responsibility. Our building supply industry will soon be normal and competitive and many new materials are being introduced. Our labour force is greatly improved in skill and numbers since the veterans have become re-established in civilian life. Also many new labour-saving tools and techniques have been introduced in recent years.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has compiled much data on housing and is conducting research on materials and methods and planning. Research is one activity of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that I should like to see expanded. Research has paid off in agriculture and I am convinced that it would pay off in housing. At this time I should like to pay a tribute to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They started from scratch not many years ago and they now have a most efficient organization. There has been a good deal of criticism by hon. members to my left about certain housing projects that went bankrupt. I think we ought to review the record. Only one per cent of the builders operating under the integrated housing scheme have gone bankrupt. Only eight builders out of six hundred have got into trouble and only 120 houses out of 14,000 units are involved. The 120 purchasers involved all have their houses completed or have received back their down payments.
As I mentioned before, the building industry practically went out of existence during the thirties and it did not have a chance to get back on its feet during the war.
When Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was given the job of administering the National Housing Act they did not have much of an industry to deal with at the start. I know for a fact that they have encouraged many people to enter the industry and have given them technical advice and help in planning. In my opinion we would not have been able to produce the number of houses we have without the well organized efforts of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation were not the only people who were fooled
[Mr. Prudham.l
by some of these builders who started in without sufficient experience or finances. The particular housing project in Calgary, which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) spent a great deal of time talking about the other night, received a loan of $13,000 from the Alberta government credit house just one month before they ceased operations.
The only way to meet the need is to build more houses. Talking does not help very much. The production and processing of materials and the necessary financial arrangements to get the finished product into use is the only solution. The industry must co-operate and respond to the challenge to produce houses for people of moderate means under the threat that if they do not do so the government has the option of participating in construction for sale or rent. Labour plays an important part in industry, and it is my opinion that labour unions should consider working a forty-four hour week while the housing emergency exists rather than the forty hour week which is common today. Now that materials are becoming more readily available, the additional four hours of work per week by the building workers could boost the over-all production of houses by as much as 10 per cent, and no one would be hurt. The workers themselves would benefit from the additional wages, and they would also benefit from the more adequate supply of housing. Tradesmen and the working classes are suffering as much as anyone else today because of the lack of housing.
The policy of the government was stated by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) on September 21, and is found in Hansard at pages 120 and 121:
Care would be exercised to see that the operations of the senior governments in this field supplement rather than replace the activity of private endeavour upon which we place the greatest reliance for large volume of house building . . . There is no desire by the dominion to enter the direct construction field.
Again I quote:
. . . the creation of conditions favourable to a large housing program by private individuals and companies. Only to the extent that housing needs are not being met, is it proposed that the dominion and the provinces will enter the field. It seems to me that only by the co-operative efforts of all levels of government and the house building industry can we maintain our high volume of new residential construction and increase it beyond its present level.
In my opinion this policy is the most practical and sane approach to the problem that we have had. The minister and his assistants are to be congratulated. The amendments are designed to implement that policy, and to make the act broad enough and flexible enough to meet the needs of any province or

municipality. The new legislation is in effect enabling legislation. It enables the municipalities and the provinces to provide utilities and services for new housing developments with the dominion assisting by bearing a large proportion of the cost. The amendments also provide for assistance to public housing projects for sale or rent with the dominion contributing a larger proportion of the costs. The responsibility is on the provinces and the municipalities to decide whether publicly sponsored projects are necessary.
The new legislation is a challenge to the industry and, in my opinion, will provide the necessary machinery for a constructive approach to the solution of the problem. The problem is too urgent and too complex for industry or government to solve alone. Only by co-operative action on the part of everyone concerned can we hope to provide adequate housing for the Canadian people. The reduction in the down payments will bring new housing within the reach of thousands of people, especially the young.
I should like to close my remarks by saying once again that the only solution to the problem is the production of more houses. To ensure this, conditions must be made favourable by the creation of serviced land and improved financial arrangements through the co-operation of all levels of government and the industry. To the members of the C.C.F. group may I say that they are probably sincere in wanting better housing conditions, but I think they lack a practical approach to the problem. Their arguments are largely based on humanitarian considerations, and they forget that the only way to build houses is by the practical application of common sense and skill. To the members of the Social Credit party I suggest that, if they are sincere in wanting better housing conditions, their efforts should be directed towards influencing the government of Alberta to cooperate under this scheme to provide serviced land so that the industry can provide the houses that are needed.
To my hon. friends of the official opposition, who have had so much to say about what the so-called enlightened government of Ontario has done, I would say that housing is constitutionally a provincial responsibility. What the Ontario government has done is but their duty, and I would suggest that if you want to promote more housing, especially in the province of Ontario, you should prevail upon the Ontario government to continue and increase their assistance. The new legislation is intended to supplement rather than replace provincial efforts. Hon. members of the official opposition have spent a great deal of time during the last few weeks supposedly
National Housing Act
defending provincial rights. It sounds rather strange to hear them finding fault now with the federal government for not doing more in the field of housing, which is a provincial responsibility. In my opinion housing is too important a problem to be tossed around for political reasons.

speechtext: What we need is genuine Canadian co-operation regardless of party and constitutional responsibilities. The new amendments to the National Housing Act now before us will provide the necessary machinery for such co-operation.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is a piece of legislation which can be very useful if it is carried forward in a spirit of co-operation, and if a wholehearted effort is made to bring together the three levels of government that can produce the results that are desired. I simply want to say in passing, in relation to the remarks that have just been made, that obviously the hon. member has not been following the discussion on this subject because the fact is that, in so far as the activities of the Ontario government are concerned, the present legislation merely replaces one part of the existing Ontario legislation, and has been welcomed by the premier of Ontario for that purpose.
I wish to say at the outset that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) has shown a commendable spirit in dealing with the provincial premiers, which is a change, and offers some hope that there will be a real spirit of co-operation under the bill now before the house. The responsibility in connection with housing is the responsibility of all the people of Canada through their representatives at the three levels of government. As far as the type of housing is concerned and the rules that apply to the actual standards of construction, such matters in the ordinary course of events come within provincial jurisdiction because of the exclusive responsibility of the provincial governments for the municipal laws of the provinces. Nevertheless the bill now before the house does offer the possibility of agreement among the three levels of government which undoubtedly will bring to any consideration of the type of housing the joint judgment and experience of those who have been associated with this work.
By virtue of the fact that a very considerable undertaking has been carried out by the national government and that in the carrying out of that program great experience has been gained, this government will be able to make a substantial contribution, not merely

National Housing Act
in the financial support that is offered but in the experience gained in the mass building that has been done under that program. In addition valuable experience will be at the disposal of the provincial governments through their municipal and other departments, such as public works, which in various ways have been associated with this activity. Above all there will be a vast store of experience, knowledge and good judgment in the possession of the municipal authorities, who during the whole development of Canada have been exercising supervision over the types of homes constructed in the urban areas where there is a concentration of building.
This is a challenge to each level of government. It is not only a challenge to bring forward constructive ideas; it is a challenge to act in the common interests of all the people of Canada. Hon. members do not need to be told from any part of the house that this is not a matter with which to play politics. That remark might well be underlined, and not necessarily directed to the official opposition, the socialists or the social credit party, because this afternoon we heard one speech that sounded as though it had reference to some bill this house has not yet seen or heard of. In that speech was drawn a picture of a new heaven and a new earth which certainly is not expressed within the four corners of this bill, and certainly was not in any way prophesied by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) in his explanation of what this act really contemplates. It may be, of course, that the hon. member was preaching for a call or trying to do a little personal prodding. The fact remains, however, that it would be very unfortunate if any attempt should be made, for political reasons, to create in the minds of the public the impression that this bill contains more than it really does.
This legislation can be the basis for effective, long-term co-operation among these three levels of government which collectively represent our people in all their many activities. That objective will be best attained if no attempt is made to create the impression that this act goes beyond what it really states. As has been very frankly explained by the minister, this is enabling legislation and nothing more, and by itself can achieve nothing except to the extent that, in the spirit of co-operation, the joint action of government at three levels brings together the experience of those who have had to do with these questions, with the common objective of giving the people not only the number of homes they need but the type of homes they need to form a foundation for a healthy, good society.

I do not want to stir up the feelings of any hon. members who may not wish to hear what was done in the province of Ontario, but in view of the fact that certain statements have been made I should like to keep the record clear on one point. This is not the first day in the history of Canada that there has been recognition on the part of those in positions of responsibility of the fact that housing is a social need. It is not the first day in the history of Canada that the necessity of giving to the people of this country an opportunity to build their own homes with a small down payment has been recognized by those in authority. I welcome, as I am sure every hon. member welcomes, the possibility of encouraging the construction of homes by reducing the amount required as a down payment; but I do want to remind some hon. members who have seen fit to be rather critical, in a friendly way, of the suggestion that there is any other wisdom or experience than that now embodied in the ranks of the present government, that other efforts have been made, and that there is very good and positive reason why in the case of Ontario, which has been mentioned, as in the case of other governments, vigorous co-operation will be forthcoming. In order that certain statements which have been made today will not remain unchallenged on the record I should like to read an editorial that appeared in The Legionary of May 1, 1948, which reviews one earlier attempt-and a not inconsiderable attempt-to deal with this subject. That attempt also dealt with certain aspects of this problem I want to place before the government and the members of the house in my later remarks. The editorial reads:
Veterans everywhere will acclaim the new housing legislation recently enacted1 in the province of Ontario to:
1.	Promote the building of more rental accommodation for veterans, by the provincial government undertaking to share with municipalities (within specified limits) costs incurred in providing serviced lots for further "wartime housing" developments.
2.	Encourage the purchase of small homes, by the provincial government undertaking to guarantee approximately $1,000 of the cash equity or down payment required of the purchaser beyond the first mortgage loan, thus eliminating one of the greatest obstacles now standing in the way of home ownership-the inability of the average would-be purchaser to finance a very high initial cash equity payment.
3.	Encourage more efficient building methods, and
4.	Provide assistance for municipalities in slum clearance projects.
Provided municipalities and lending institutions co-operate to the maximum in making this new legislation fulfil its intended purposes, Ontario will in all probability now see a house-building boom of unprecedented proportions, bringing renewed hope for every home-seeking veteran in that province.

In this new housing legislation, the Ontario government is blazing new trails out of which might materialize the long-awaited over-all plan for the successful solution of the housing problem in every part of the dominion which the Legion has been pressing for so hard ever since the war ended.
Now, that editorial in The Legionary brieflly reviewed the attempt made by the government of that province to deal with the subject. I only mention this now to point out that this is a subject which has been engaging the thought and the concern, not only of the government of Ontario, but of every government in Canada. I feel sure that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply would be the first in this house to say that he had found nothing but a desire on the part of the provincial premiers to further any effort seeking the effective co-operation of all levels of government to advance the development of housing in Canada.
There is one feature of the Ontario provision which I should like to mention. I have said that the attempt by that provincial government was not inconsiderable, and I think that is a fair statement. The commitment made under this bill in regard to the co-operative plan is approximately $50 million. The Ontario government committed itself to a program involving $35 million, so that it took rather extensive steps to enter this field as far as it could at that time. This bill, of course, goes beyond that in other ways and offers wider opportunities of co-operation which will, undoubtedly, expand as time goes on.
One of the things mentioned in this editorial, and which I should like to put before the house and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, is the importance of encouraging the employment of new types of building. I believe that has already been mentioned by the hon. member who spoke immediately before me, and who, I understand, has had practical building experience. He mentioned the fact that new types of construction provide new opportunities for building homes. I imagine that nearly every member has already seen some of the new types of homes that have been constructed but which, for one reason or another, have not been generally employed in these programs. I can think of many of them. I feel sure that the minister has seen a most interesting development on the north shore of lake Superior at Terrace. Within the last three years a new community has grown up out of the virgin forest and today it is a beautiful town with homes that would attract attention anywhere. The cost of those houses was much lower than would have been the case in any urban or suburban development elsewhere, because they were
National Housing Act
built under one plan with special types of construction and with the actual prefabrication done on the site.
The figures for the cost of construction suggested that those houses were being built and could be sold at less than two-thirds of the price of similar homes in many cities and towns in Canada. I have seen other developments. There is one not far away at Marathon, and I have no doubt there are others in other parts of Canada. With the possibility of radiant heating, with the possibility of metal frames, with new opportunities for insulation and for prefabrication of mass-produced houses, there are great opportunities for lowering the cost and improving the standards of the houses themselves. I would hope that the plans which are made will provide for the encouragement of new developments of that kind.
As the minister of reconstruction doubtless knows, one of the features of the plan to which I have referred was the financial support of new types of construction which demonstrated their practical possibilities. It would be unfortunate if, at this stage, we did not make every possible use of what the builders have learned from the experience of these past years.
There is one feature of this bill which I believe might well be given consideration, and that is the interest rate. Again, I am not putting it forward as a basis of unfavourable comparison, but nevertheless I would remind the minister that under the Ontario provision for reducing the down payment, the loan guaranteed under the Ontario plan was provided at 3i per cent. As that was on a second mortgage, I do think that the government might give consideration to the possibility of an interest rate lower than the 4J per cent on the amount that is advanced. It is true that this figure might contemplate the desirability of having a certain safety margin for those cases in which the rental will not be collected.
As I understand, it is the intention of the government to take a calculated risk in accepting losses in construction, and it is for that very reason that provision is made for the joint responsibility of the dominion and provincial governments. Under this plan, therefore, I do not think the interest rate should be fixed at a level which will provide anything in the nature of an insurance fund against the possibility of loss on any of the other payments. I would urge that consideration be given to the lowering of that figure. I point out that, under the other plan to which I have referred, a lower interest rate was charged and is now being paid on some 11,000 second mortgages which were arranged.

National Housing Act
I do wish to emphasize this feature of the bill that is before the house. I do not intend to embark on the discussion of a subject which can be discussed on another occasion, but rentals have a bearing on this subject that cannot possibly be overlooked in examining the effectiveness of any plan of this kind. First of all, there is the question as to whether rentals will themselves be at a level that will make the purchase of homes seem relatively attractive.
There is also the fact that a considerable part of the building of homes in Canada in the past has been done for the purpose of investment. Undoubtedly there are landlords whose conduct is open to the most severe criticism. But let us also remember that there are many landlords who, in relation to their tenants, have acted in a manner which the tenants themselves would be the first to say has been fair. Let us also remember who some of these landlords are. Many of them are widows who have been left with homes which are larger than they can use and which perhaps represent their largest evidence of personal security. There are other landlords who have built their own homes while they were younger and then as their family has grown or they have felt that they wanted another home, they have built another house; they have kept the first one and have rented it. These are investments which, under our system, should not be discouraged if that system is to continue.
I hope no one will seek to interpret what I have said as any defence of or excuse for those who have abused the opportunity that has existed on many occasions during the present critical demand for housing. I think it is time, however, that we were all fair enough to recognize that every landlord is not a man or woman of evil design nor is every tenant a saint. In the balance of human experience, in every relationship there are those who present their problems in any of these tasks that must be undertaken. The needs of the tenants must be respected. The right of tenants not to have improper rentals charged under the compelling demand of necessity and the shortage of houses, and also the right of fair landlords to have some assurance of what their rights are as well, should be recognized in dealing with any of these plans. Anything else produces bad results for tenants as well as for landlords.
One of the objections that are expressed to-what has recently happened with regard to rents is the uncertainty and confusion which will have its impact on this whole question of housing as well. I am not going

to enlarge on that matter at this point, because this subject can be discussed in complete detail on another occasion; but I suggest that it will be well for the government to remember that, in approaching the provincial authorities and the municipal authorities, they are going to be asked what the situation is with regard to rentals. I hope they will be in a position to give a much more satisfactory answer than can be given today, because all over this country now tenants are disturbed and are naturally resentful of what they regard as the complete repudiation of undertakings to protect their rights. Others who thought that they were benefiting in some way are equally confused as to the extent to which their rights are being recognized.
These day-by-day clarifications, which I believe is the official word used to describe them, and which represent new efforts to cure the incurable, are in themselves only contributing difficulties in the way of that necessary measure of co-operation. While on this occasion we cannot go further in reaching any positive conclusion on the matter, may I say that the government would be well advised to start all over again on these rental measures that they have so recently undertaken and to seek to follow a course that can be understood and that recognizes the general obligation, under circumstances of this kind, to treat fairly all those with whom they deal. Then one of the questions that will be raised can be answered, because undoubtedly that question will be asked.
In some remarks that were made today, it was stated that the number of houses will depend upon the attitude of the provincial governments in relation to the municipalities in working out these plans. It is going to depend on the attitude of the dominion government, not only in regard to this particular bill but in regard to the wider field of dominion-provincial co-operation.
The question was raised tonight as to the constant emphasis that is placed upon provincial rights. That comment was based upon an obvious misunderstanding of the arguments which have really been presented. Those who have emphasized the need for dominion-provincial understanding on the widest possible basis have been doing so in the belief that it is essential that the three levels of government in this country ought to know what their responsibilities are, what their ability is to carry out those responsibilities as well. The argument has been based upon the contention that a government cannot carry out those legislative and administrative responsibilities which it thinks it should carry out unless it also knows whether, and

to what extent, it can raise the revenue necessary for that purpose. One of the things that have been emphasized over and over again in this house and outside of it is the need for clarification of the relationship between the dominion government and the provincial governments. Mr. Speaker, after the humorous interjection of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), I now wish to mention another point which was introduced earlier. It is this, that emphasis was placed in some remarks made today on the objective being set. I believe these were the words, "We set an objective; we reached that objective."
Let us keep this in a clear sense of proportion: This is enabling legislation. This is legislation which will best be advanced in the interests of the people of Canada if it does not start with attempts being made to create the impression that the building being done under it will be done by agencies of the dominion government, entirely, or even in a major degree.
The remarks to which I am referring were not those of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters), who has made it clear that he believes that the major building program should be carried out by the building contractors of this country, operating under the broad provisions of agreements that can be made.
The reason I mention this lies in the fact that, if the impression is created that this is a bill only to provide buildings or mainly to provide buildings which will be built by a government agency, it will not receive the support it should receive. Because what the people of this country want is encouragement to those who can buy their homes to build those homes according to their own desires. And it is the duty of the government-and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has indicated a full recognition of this-to join in meeting the need for homes facing all our people.
There are too many people in Canada who are still badly housed. There are too many people who even yet can find no homes. There are still too many people who are

National Housing Act
badly clothed, and there are too many who are badly fed. But that condition is not going to be met by any single bill or by any simple device. That represents a problem that reaches into the wider field of education, of social services and of all these other things.
Let us be sure that in this particular case the words of the minister are remembered, and that it is recognized that, except for the special plans indicated in his remarks, this mainly contemplates encouragement to private contractors to build homes to be purchased by the people of Canada. And as was pointed out by one hon. member in his remarks today, by the fact that in the very nature of their activities many people move from place to place, it is required that there shall always be a certain number of homes available for rental, quite apart from what we may describe under the over-all expression of low-rental housing.
Having said that, however, I feel sure there is not a single member in the house who does not agree the hope should be that as many of our people as possible are able to buy their homes, and in that way to establish the sound foundation of their family life, with that measure of personal association, personal interest and personal pride in the home that has so much to do with the life that is the basis of our society.
In all this, the success or otherwise of this bill when it becomes law will depend upon wholehearted co-operation among the three levels of government. Let us remember that this government can pass only enabling legislation. But it can contribute experience, and so can the provincial governments; and in the end it will be the municipal governments which, with their services and their various municipal bylaws, will have most to do with any homes that are built.
Above all, in the planning of these projects which will emerge from this legislation, let us do all we can to make sure that in this great and vast country of ours we do assure as much land as is possible for every one of these homes, that we make them as attractive as possible, and that we encourage the very highest and most permanent type of building consistent with the availability of supplies and the money available. Let us do this so that not only may we be providing shelter for today but that we may be providing homes for the years ahead, homes that will really be homes in the very finest sense of the word.
