Mr. Speaker, I shall not trespass long upon the time of the house. However in my riding of Parkdale

the housing situation is of a critical nature, and I feel I should make some remarks not only about the amendment but about certain things which in my view the amendment fails to accomplish.
We all know that not so very long ago the matter of buying a house was entirely a man's private business. If he could afford to buy a house, he bought one; if he could not afford to buy one, he did not buy one. No one cared what he did. However, in recent years, as has been stated so repeatedly, it has become clear that housing has become a distinctly social problem. It is realized that poor housing can contribute to overcrowded conditions which bring about disease and ills of that nature. It can create poor marital relations, cause the breaking up of homes and contribute to juvenile delinquency.
The original Dominion Housing Act was passed in 1935. The National Housing Act was first passed in 1938. That act provided for a reduction in the down payment on houses and permitted amortized payments at lower rates of interest. That act proved most helpful and a great deal of housing was built under it. It is interesting to note the tremendous progression in social security trends and thinking that we have witnessed in our own day. With your permission I should like to review briefly the act and the amendments to see just what we have accomplished.
It will be noted that the act is divided into six parts. Part I deals largely with housing for home owners and provides for the usual 80 per cent loan with interest at four and a half per cent and 30 year amortization. The housing corporation's share is not to exceed 25 per cent and the corporation may guarantee to the lending institution up to 15 per cent of their share. Under that home owners part we now have provision for additional loans of one-sixth more if the price is fair and reasonable, and I shall have something to say on that later on.
Under part I provision is made for the integrated housing plan with which I think most hon. members are familiar. As far as I have personally witnessed the operation of this plan, it appears to be available only to veterans, but I would hope that this will soon be extended right across the board. I feel that if the many restrictions which have been placed on integrated housing were withdrawn this would be greatly appreciated by the building industry.
The third part of part I deals with cooperative building. This is an intricate, detailed matter and I do not propose to go into it at all. The terms are set forth in the amendment.

Part II of the act deals with rental housing and some seven different plans are provided. The first is the ordinary joint loan made to the builder who erects housing units for rent. The second is the guaranteed rental plan with which most hon. members are familiar. The rents are agreed upon between the corporation and the builder for a period of three years and are guaranteed for the term of the loan, not exceeding thirty years. The guarantee is not to exceed 85 per cent of the rents which are determined for the first three years.
The third plan provides for the setting up of limited dividend housing companies. Under that plan the rents are agreed upon and there is the usual ratio between rents and the income of the people who are to occupy the housing units. A 90 per cent loan is provided for with interest at three per cent, the term being for the useful life of the buildings or not more than 50 years. This plan is usually carried out by a corporation especially incorporated for that purpose. I have seen this in operation and I believe it is a most useful feature of the act.
The next plan provides for housing for special industries. I have not been in a position to witness the operation of any of these plans by mining, lumbering, logging or fishing companies. The act provides for an 80 per cent loan at four per cent, not exceeding a 15-year term. The fifth part provides for institutional housing corporations and institutional holding companies. This is the scheme whereby the lending institution as designated by the act can set up a low-rental scheme.
The sixth part provides for institutional land improvement schemes. An institution may take over a block of land, thoroughly service it and then offer it for sale to builders. The only advantage to the lending institution which has a guarantee for five years from the government of a return of two per cent is the hope and probability that it will sell land to builders who will obtain loans from the institution. This scheme has been quite successful and 1 have no doubt it will be used more as time goes on.
The seventh scheme under this part provides for slum clearance, the clearance of what is sometimes called blighted or substandard areas. We have seen this scheme worked out in certain cases. There are not many ridings where slums are a problem and therefore this scheme would be applicable only to a limited number of ridings in Canada. Under this scheme the municipality acquires the land and after clearing it sells it to a limited dividend housing corporation. The dominion government makes grants not exceeding one-half of the difference between
National Housing Act
the cost of acquiring and clearing and the sale price to the limited dividend housing corporation.
Under part III of the act provision is made for rural housing. The provisions here are similar to those in part I. Under part IV provision is made for home improvement and home extension loans. Provision is made for loans up to $2,500 for single units, and $2,500 for the first and $1,250 for each subsequent unit in a multiple unit scheme. This part has not yet been proclaimed.
Under part V provision is made for housing research and community planning. This provides for the expenditure of up to $5 million on research and community planning. This provision somewhat overlaps the $5 million which can be provided under part III which deals with rural housing. Under this part experiments in plumbing, heating and other component parts of housing could be carried on.
Part VI is the general part which gives very broad powers to supplement the more specific powers set out in the other sections. The amendment section 35 will give additional powers.
I have some suggestions to make which possibly are of a critical nature, but I do feel that some of the provisions of this act will have to be extended. There are many things which are not perfect at the present time. Section 5, subsection 2, provides that the corporation may for the purposes of part III of the act prescribe the manner in which the cost of construction of a house or of a housing project shall be estimated, and by whom and in what manner the appraisal of the value of the house shall be made.
The definition section states that lending value means the estimated cost of construction or cost of conversion, or the appraised value, whichever is less, of a house or housing project. Anyone familiar with the working of the National Housing Act is only too well aware that there is a great distinction between lending value as defined in the act and the sale price or market value. Therefore when one speaks of an 80 per cent loan it will be obvious to every member of the house that it is most important and vital that there be some close relationship between the lending value and the market value. Otherwise the 80 per cent advance may not be of any great assistance in helping people to purchase homes.
I think the act has been administered with great fairness in the past, but I suggest that it will have to be administered with a greater breadth of vision. I do not for one moment criticize the attitude which has been adopted by the president of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He has been in the

National Housing Act
position where he was given an act to administer. He has been told the money is available for loans, and accordingly he has made them. He is a sound businessman and does not care to lose money. If the government fails to provide more housing they must to a certain minor extent subsidize housing in this manner. I feel it has been unfair to put the whole burden on the president of the housing corporation. I think the government might well take this matter under advisement, as they have under part III, and that the government should lay down the policy from time to time in that connection instead of leaving it to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the officials thereof. I make this suggestion, and I think it might be desirable that a further amendment to the act be passed in the near future to bring this matter directly under the government rather than having it handled by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
We must administer the act in such a way that the distinction between lending value and market value will be very slight. Otherwise we are not going to give the help to the purchasers of homes that we obviously hope to give. Turning to the additional one-sixth loan which is now being provided under the bill, it will be recalled by all members of the house that this loan can only be made if the purchase price is considered to be fair and reasonable. I am afraid I must take exception to an amendment worded in that fashion. It is my personal belief that to say that the one-sixth loan will only be advanced if the purchase price is fair and reasonable has no relevancy. I cannot see how the reasonableness or unreasonableness of the purchase price has any relation to the loan. If it will make it any easier for a person to buy a house, I do not see that it matters whether the corporation considers the price reasonable or unreasonable. Surely if the purchaser has sufficient money to pay the unreasonable price the government will help him to the extent of extending the extra one-sixth loan and making the house that much more easily obtainable. At the same time the government is not taking any more risk than they would with a normal house.
I have always felt that the important thing to any purchaser of a house is the down payment. I think most members will agree, if they have had any experience in real estate, that it is the down payment that is interesting to the average young married couple, and to many older people. I have always felt that, instead of having the present system, surely the loan should be calculated to help the person to buy the house, and that it would be better to have a graduated

down payment in relation to the purchase price. I throw out that suggestion. I have talked to many people about it. Provided that the down payment is made reasonably sufficient to ensure an adequate stake in the house, I think that is something that could well be put into effect. In that case I would agree it might well be advisable to add that the price must be fair and reasonable. For instance, if you say that a $500 down payment is needed for a $6,000 house, a $750 down payment for a $7,500 house, and so on, .1 think you are getting closer to the root of the problem because it is the down payment that is the killer to the average young married couple trying to buy a house.
I can assure anyone who feels that $500 is a small stake in a $6,000 house, that to any young married couple who are just getting started $500 is a lot of money and a big stake, and that they are going to fight very hard to keep that house.
There is one other suggestion I should like to make. It is something that is coming eventually. I do not think there is any great urgency at the moment, but eventually we will have to amortize houses over a longer period of time. The reason I do not think it is so urgent at the moment is that I have not much doubt that in the next six months or a year all the available labour forces and supplies will be poured into housing in any event, and those houses will be sold. The market will readily absorb them, but I think eventually we will have to amortize these loans over a longer period. It is not only important that the down payment be small; it is equally important that the carrying charges be small. Provided the house is of adequate construction to stand longer amortization, I think it will be entirely desirable. As I said before, however, I feel in the next year all the available men and materials will be used, and that there will be no slackening of the market for houses.
It may be that at the end of another year it will be desirable to re-examine the act to see how it is working and readjust our viewpoint towards it. I can assure the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) that the amendments have my most enthusiastic support. I think they are decidedly a great step in the right direction. I think we will probably find there are some inadequacies, but I have no doubt they will be corrected.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter we are discussing this evening, and indeed we have discussed it all day, is not something in the nature of the principle of stare decisis nor even the question of the Combines Investigation Act. It is

a matter which is known and understood and is of the greatest importance, I may say, to all Canadians. The question of housing is one which people from all over Canada not only know, but know to their great cost these days from the point of view of the necessity existing for increased housing units.
I do not think that we can emphasize the matter of housing too much because, if I may use outworn words, housing is of the greatest importance in the making of good citizens not only in Canada but all over the world. Home environment to a very great measure molds the future children of the world. The last outworn remark I might make is that criminal tendencies may very well be developed as a result of poor housing conditions. I think that is realized by all hon. members of the house, and the interest they have displayed in the legislation is sufficient proof of the importance with which they view it.
The bill that we are discussing is, as the minister said when he first introduced the resolution, an enabling act. It gives the dominion government power to discuss with provincial governments, and through them with municipalities and, as he said on September 21, with other public bodies. I take it that "other public bodies" would be bodies other than provincial governments and municipalities such as housing corporations. I hope to refer to that later.
I must say that the bill appears to be a very sensible approach to the problem. Its provisions, read with the act as it stands today, seem pretty conclusive. The only question I have in my own mind is whether it goes far enough. I am not trying to criticize the government in this regard; in fact I disagree with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Prudham), who referred to hon. members to his left who were criticizing. I considered that what I heard of this discussion was constructive criticism. I do not believe anything destructive was uttered by an hon. member. As far as I could judge anything said even by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who spoke at length on this subject, was purely constructive.
The hon. member for Edmonton West referred to one other matter. He said that constitutionally housing was a provincial matter. I must say I entirely agree with the statement by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) a few moments ago that housing is the responsibility of the whole Canadian people. It is not the responsibility of the provinces, of the municipalities or even of the dominion government; it can be solved only by all the people working together. That, I am sure, will be one of the important
National Housing Act
results of the tour made by the minister before this legislation was introduced. I am quite certain he has put a great deal of work into that tour. He paid Newfoundland a very real tribute by making our province one of his first visits. Incidentally, in respect to the timing of his visit-I am sure it was pure coincidence-he came just before the election, and I can assure you that the Liberal party lost no votes as a result. Nevertheless his visit was very welcome, and from his correspondence with the premier of my province I can see the minister is really getting his teeth into our problem in Newfoundland, and of course the problem of Canada as a whole. I should like to join other hon. members in saying that as far as I can see the minister really is trying to do a job to the best of his ability. We realize, of course, that he has had a hard row to hoe in this matter. I would not go so far as to say, as an hon. member said some time ago, that the minister has been handed a lemon, but his has been a hard job because housing legislation has been before many parliaments. The problem is not new, but as far as we can judge he is really getting down and tackling it manfashion.
I do not want to delay the house too long this evening, but there are a few points on which I should like some enlightenment. There is the matter of slum clearance. On October 31 my confrere the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) asked whether slum clearance came within the purview of the act, and I believe the answer was that it was provided for in the general act. But then I saw in Hansard of September 21 a question asked by the hon. member for Eglinton:
In the first place, is any specific assistance contemplated in connection with slum clearance?
The answer by the minister at that time was:
The sections now in the act with respect to slum clearance are quite clear. I do not believe the statement I have just made is debatable at the moment, but there will be a resolution before the house rela-. tively soon, upon which occasion I should be glad to discuss all these matters.
That question has not been discussed since, and I do not know whether it is dealt with in the act. So when the minister speaks I hope he will refer to this point. I am particularly anxious about it because we have a great problem in connection with slum clearance in St. John's and in fact throughout many towns in Newfoundland. I understand an announcement has been made that construction of some five hundred houses is to be undertaken within the next few months in St. John's. I shall be glad to hear that this is so.

National Housing Act
The other matter I am particularly interested in is what is to become of the St. John's Housing Corporation. When the minister was in Newfoundland he visited the corporation and saw something of its work and what is needed. I might just tell hon. members that something like $6 million has been invested by the provincial government and the municipality, and that the corporation now owes some $1 million to the municipality and $5 million to the provincial government. That project includes the most modem housing; it is located on some 800 acres of expropriated land, with a modern sewage system and modern roads. As of October 1 some 240 houses had been constructed and under construction and ten apartment buildings containing 92 apartments, making a total of 332 housing units. Without money that corporation is not going to be able to carry on. This matter was discussed by the original delegation that came here in 1947, at which time a committee was appointed consisting of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), Mr. D. B. Mansur of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the premier of Newfoundland and myself. Since I had been connected with the housing corporation I presented a brief on the matter to the committee of cabinet, outlining the work of the corporation since its formation in 1944 and the need for more financial assistance. If I might read from the volume tabled in parliament in December 1947, containing the report of the meeting between the delegation and the cabinet, this reference appears:
Would it be possible to receive a grant for this purpose . . .
That is, the purpose of the corporation.
... or, if not, could any form of financial assistance be made available to the corporation in the event of union?
The answer at that time was:
In reply, it was pointed out that under present facilities available there was no manner in which the dominion could take over the position now held by Newfoundland and the city of St. John's in respect to the St. John's Housing Corporation. It falls within the category of a provincial-municipal housing project for which no assistance by way of loans, subsidies or rent reduction funds are presently available from the dominion to a province and/or a municipality.
On that point, as the minister stated, this bill deals with public bodies apart from municipalities and provinces; and I would submit that public bodies might very well include this housing corporation. So I wonder if under this legislation any financial assistance might be given the St. John's Housing Corporation, or what is the plan for the future

in that connection. From reading the bill I am not very clear whether or not funds can be obtained under it by the corporation.
The only other matter I wish to stress at this time is the question of providing low-rental housing, not only for all of Canada but particularly for St. John's, because that is the only place I can use as an example. I realize that if the necessity for low-rental housing is great in the place that I know best, it must be even greater in other parts of Canada. I believe provision is made for that in the bill. It strikes me, however, that with the relaxation of rent controls so recently announced there should be an even more intensive effort put into effect a low-rental housing scheme. I shall not transgress the Speaker's ruling by talking about rentals, but if rents are going to have the lid taken off then something in the nature of a low-rental housing scheme must be put into operation at the earliest possible moment.
I should like to mention that I was quite taken with the remarks of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) about rural housing and the fact that no provision had been made in this bill for the promotion of rural housing. It strikes me that is one of the most important phases of the housing situation. If it has been overlooked, it should certainly be included in this bill or a suitable bill covering that matter should be presented. You remember that the old song asked the question "How are you going to keep them down on the farm?" There is only one way you can keep people on the farm and that is by providing rural communities with the facilities that are usually associated with living in a city. It should not be too difficult to provide those facilities. Certainly, I think it is the direct responsibility of the government to provide proper facilities for rural dwellers, just as it is to provide houses for urban dwellers.
I do not see any mention in the bill of veterans' preference. It strikes me rather forcibly that this has always been to the forefront and I do not know why it has been dropped. It would appear to be worthy of consideration, because from the discussions I have had with people in Ottawa the need for veterans houses is just as great as it ever was. I shall conclude with these remarks, Mr. Speaker, so that it will be possible for the minister to close the debate, as he is anxious that the bill go into committee tonight.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Just before the minister closes the debate, I Wish to take a moment to say a few words. I shall be brief so that the

minister will have time to close the debate tonight. In what I shall say I may not be adding to what has been said during the course of this debate, but it does seem to me that it is worth while in part to sum up what has been said, and in part to place before the house the objectives with respect to this housing problem.
As I see it, there are three. First of all, and perhaps the most important problem facing us, is the need for subsidized low-rental housing. It is important not just to get the phrase into the minister's statement, but to get large-scale subsidized low-rental housing projects under way at the earliest possible moment.
The second objective which I feel we must not overlook is, to use the words of my colleague the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), to realize that getting the down payment reduced to a smaller amount is not enough. The fact of the matter is that a great many of our people could not afford to buy houses today even if there were no down payment. Steps have to be taken to bring down the cost of good homes and to improve the living standards of our people so that they can own good homes.
The third objective which I think should be kept before us, even though it may be a long-range one, is to realize that we have not solved the problem of housing just because we reach a point where every Canadian is under a roof of some kind. For example, I think of the trip that I make when I go to and from the place where I live in this city. When I do not get a ride with one of my friends, I take the 'R' streetcar which goes out Albert street and down Preston street. A good many people live along those streets and I see those houses every morning as I come down here. Those people have a roof over their heads, but it is not satisfactory housing in which at least half of them are living. That is the case all over this country. A tremendous job lies ahead of us. This is a social as well as an economic problem.
We must not think we have solved the problem merely because people have a roof over their head. This is a field in which research can be undertaken and in which new types of home construction are long overdue. I feel that it is one of the most important problems to which we must give our attention. I hope that this parliament, and whatever government is in power during the next few years, will accept it as a major objective to provide good and adequate housing for all the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage I wish to be very brief. 1 am most anxious that the legislation should pass this house as quickly as possible because, among other things, it will be necessary for most of the provincial governments to pass legislation which will enable them to participate in the dominion-provincial program embodied in this bill. I wish, therefore, to commend all members who have taken part in this debate for the high order of their remarks.
After talking to all the provincial governments I was able to say that, without exception, they realized the gravity of the problem and showed a real desire to come to grips with it. I now can say that all members who participated in the debate fully reflected the attitude of all members in the house in their view of the importance of this problem of housing to all Canadians. I thought we had a very good cross-section of the general attitude towards the problem. It ranged all the way from those who opposed any element of subsidization to those who felt that a full program of subsidization was the important approach to this question.
I should like, of course, to deal in detail with the points raised by the various members, but that would take too long. There was some putting straight of the record tonight with respect to the contribution made to the housing problem by the province of Ontario, especially by the leader of the opposition. Let me be among the first to say that Ontario is to be highly commended for what it has done. There is no doubt about the contribution that province has made. I think it must be said that the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) perhaps somewhat overstated the achievement when he said that the 10,000 houses on which second mortgages were applied were built only because second mortgages were made available. I do not wish in any way to detract, however, and I wish to make that clear. As one example, though, I would refer to the 100 houses that were built in Manor Park, which were completed and fully occupied before the home owners applied for the second mortgage. And he referred to the fact that this government was two and a half years behind the Ontario government in introducing the second mortgage practice of reducing down payment. As I understand it, the act in Ontario was passed in May, 1948, and the first loan was made in August, 1948, which is considerably less than two and half years ago.
I wish to commend especially the vigorous speeches made by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) and the hon. member for

National Housing Act
Halton (Mr. Cleaver) who, I thought, pointed the way to what can be done by all members of this house and a great many people in this country with regard to a solution of the housing problem. He gave me an opportunity I have sought for some time. I thank him for the remarks he made about the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and would add my own to them, for the splendid service they have given in working on this problem and in adding so greatly to the stock of housing units in Canada today.
One other word I would say is in connection with rural housing. I think the point was raised by the hon. members for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) and Melfort (Mr. Wright) and their point was well taken. They were a bit apprehensive that perhaps existing legislation might not do what it should do for the rural segment of our economy, and one might easily get that impression. I understand there are some 700,000 farms in Canada and, roughly speaking, there is one house on each farm. By and large, new housing is not the problem facing the farmers today; it is a matter of improvements and, in some cases, extensions. Where there is a demand for loans for new farmhouses, those loans, other things being equal, are forthcoming under section 14 of the act. Where improvements are necessary, facilities for borrowing are available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act administered by the Department of Finance. We of course agree with the hon. member for Melfort about the quality of farmhouses which, in many instances, could well be improved. But the fact is that supplies have not been available to promote large improvement programs. That is the very reason why the home improvement section of the act has not been proclaimed so far.
Since the hon. member comes from Saskatchewan, one of the prairie provinces, I will tell him that there is a prairie farm research committee to which the federal government contributes 55 per cent of the finances required and to which each of the three prairie governments contribute 15 per cent. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the three provincial governments and the three provincial universities have seven major projects under way now for research and development, on problems relating to rural housing. I will tell him also that there is much more on that subject in the annual report of the corporation, and if he wishes additional information I shall be pleased to see that he gets it.
Just before I resume my seat-and I do not wish to dwell any longer on speeches made by hon. members-I would say just one word to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Prudham) who in making his maiden speech
dealt with a subject about which he knows so much from his own practical experience. I want to say to him, and to all hon. members who took part in the debate, how highly constructive I have found their words. I appreciate the attitude they have reflected towards the bill for which we are seeking the approval of the house.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As was announced some days ago, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will be here tomorrow and the first order of business will be a motion by him that votes numbers 51 to 70 inclusive in the main estimates, 1949-50, and numbers 766 to 779 inclusive in the further supplementary estimates, 1949-50, be withdrawn from the committee of supply and be referred to the standing committee on external affairs, saving always the powers of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public moneys. If the debate on this motion be concluded before six o'clock, we will move one step forward with Bill No. 149, respecting bankruptcy. I understand this bill has no political significance. It is a technical bill and a long one. I am furthermore informed that it will take quite a long time before the committee on banking and commerce. We should therefore like to have it advanced one stage tomorrow, if possible.

May I ask if it is the government's intention to press this bill to adoption at this session? The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated that we were aiming at prorogation by December 3. This is a long and involved bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand that most of the work on this bill will be done in the committee on banking and commerce. If we can get it before that committee, we shall then have to wait for the report of the committee. If it came back, perhaps we would have a chance to have it adopted. It has been in the Senate for two or three sessions, I believe. It has been modified. Expert witnesses have been heard. If the bill did not pass this session, it would have to go back to the Senate again. We shall therefore do our utmost to have it back from the committee on banking and commerce during this session.
